subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In rising to resume the debate, I wish at the outset to congratulate the mover (Mr. Gobeil) and the seconder (Mr. Barber) of the address on the splendid speeches they made, reflecting great credit not only upon themselves but also upon the constituencies which they have the honour to represent.
I listened very carefully the other day for over four hours to the speech of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and I was very much disappointed when he was through. During that entire time there was no constructive policy, there was nothing put forward by the right hon. gentleman but fault-finding. He found fault with the present administration, and I began to wonder whether these men sitting on the treasury benches, grown old in the service of their country, were attempting to pull down and ruin the reputation of Canada, or whether after all they did not have some business judgment and there was not something that they had done that could find approval from the leader of the opposition.
The right hon. gentleman made the statement that we had a million on relief and a million and a half unemployed, a statement which is not borne out by the facts. I have received a report from the Deputy Minister of Labour giving the figures for the months of November and December of 1932 and 1933 respectively as to the number of families on
rMr. Lapointe.]
relief, and that I submit is the fairest way of estimating the number of people on relief in this country. A bread-winner is out of work and goes on relief. He may have a wife and family of half a dozen children, but it is not right to suggest that his wife and children should be numbered amongst the unemployed. He is the head of one family, one bread-winner who has gone on relief. I am therefore giving the number of families that have been on relief, which as I say is the fairest way of arriving at an honest conclusion.
In November, 1933, there were 17,783 less families on relief than there were in November, 1932, and in December, 1933, there were 25,679 less families on relief than there were in December, 1932. That shows conclusively that we are to-day in a better and not in a worse condition than we were a year ago. I cannot understand therefore what good purpose is to be served by public men decrying and blackening the reputation of their own country at a time when every loyal citizen is straining every effort to pull the Canadian people out of the morass and entanglement in which they have found themselves.
Yesterday we listened to another speech, this time from the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart), in which he denounced the tariff policies of this government. He waxed very eloquent and worked himself into a great fever, holding up his hands in holy horror. I thought at the time he was longing for a tambourine or a little tin drum on which to beat the death knell of protection. Whatever it may be, he charged the Prime Minister and the Conservative party with being responsible for all the ills that exist in this country at the present time, and especially did he charge that the policies of the present government were responsible for our unemployment situation. These statements are not borne out by the facts. I claim that the greatest factor in causing unemployment in Canada was the unbusinesslike immigration policy of the Liberal government from 1921 to 1930. During those years they brought in 1,187,319 immigrants against the protests of the provinces in which those people were placed and against the business judgment of our most able Canadians. In the last two years during which they were responsible for immigration, and at a time when our own men were unemployed and when every man who had any insight into our future knew it was a wrong policy, they brought in 331,000 immigrants, of whom 99,000 who came in during the last year were single men who immediately went on relief. Had the former Liberal administration followed the same

The Address-Mr. Thompson (Lanark)
immigration policy that is being pursued by the present government and restricted immigration to the extent we have done there would be no unemployment and no need for relief here to-day.
When the present government took office they found the markets of the world largely closed to the Canadian exporters. France, Germany, Italy, that formerly took millions of bushels of our wheat, had raised their tariffs to a prohibitive height. The United States to which we had sent a large quantity of our produce had from time to time raised their tariffs making it impossible for us to do business with them with any degree of satisfaction. In 1922 the Fordney-McCumber tariff hit the Canadian exporter a serious blow, and this was followed in 1930 by the Hawley-Smoot tariff, making it impossible for the Canadian exporter to do business with the nation to the south of us. The point I would emphasize is that these European and United States markets were lost to the Canadian exporter between 1921 and 1930 when our hon. friends opposite were in power. I do not blame the Liberal government of that day for the tariff policies of foreign countries but I do blame them for taking knock after knock lying down. I blame them for sitting with folded hands while the markets of the world were being closed to Canadian products and allowing the Canadian market to be the dumping ground for the surplus products of every other nation in the world. Further I say that the tariff policy of the present government has kept Canada solvent and that by securing in the British market a substantial preference for the Canadian exporter they have safeguarded the Canadian producer and protected the Canadian farmer from the very worst effects of the present world depression. The imperial trade agreements made at Ottawa and the general policy of the present government have combined to wipe out a heavy adverse trade balance and to replace it with a favourable trade balance of $136,000,000. This has been one of the greatest achievements of the present government. Notwithstanding the fact that economic nationalism has been paralysing international trade, the Canadian exporter found a haven from the general chaos of world trade in a sheltered market of the British Empire where, in the best market in the world for agricultural and other primary products, the present government has secured for him a preference.
There is nothing that affects Canada to a greater extent than the repayment of her foreign debts and her future borrowing in the foreign money market, and judging from our experience in the past I am convinced there should be set up in Canada a board of 74726-10
financial experts to whom all prospective borrowers should be asked to submit their propositions before being permitted to enter the foreign money market. Such a board would safeguard us against excessive, borrowings and protect us from those dangerous terms of repayment that have characterized so many of our loans in the past. The whole economic system of the world is to-day labouring under a nightmare of debt that is paralyzing and demoralizing those who receive the loan as well as those who make it.
We have to the south of us a great nation of 130,000,000 people experimenting with a species of dictatorship, feverishly endeavouring to raise themselves out of the morass of economic and financial entanglements in which they find themselves involved. We wish them well; we trust they will be successful because we realize that the future welfare and prosperity of this dominion is inseparably associated with that of the United States. We are neighbours living close together and what affects the one will always materially affect the other. But while they are strenuously endeavouring to bring about new conditions and a better social life in their country, they seem to forget all about the debt, and I should like to call to their remembrance this fact, that the same prayer which says "Thy kingdom come" says also "Forgive us our debts as we forgive our debtors."
Our hon. friends opposite during former sessions in the house and on the stump throughout the country have apparently taken great delight in comparing prices of farm produce since 1930 with what they were prior to that date. They seem to forget that no government can control world prices, and that the inexorable law of supply and demand rules the world to-day as it ever did. The only comparison that can be fairly made is between the prices of farm products in Canada and the prices in other countries. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the prices of agricultural products in Canada since 1930 have been higher in comparison with those in other countries than they were during the regime of our hon. friends opposite. Take prices to-day; we have pork selling on the hoof in Montreal and Toronto at 10 cents, while in Chicago it is selling at only 4 cents. The best sign of the recovery from the depression is to be found in the fact that agricultural products are continually rising in price. Canada is essentially an agricultural country, and until the farmers of Canada receive a fair remuneration for their labour and the capital they have invested there will be no real prosperity in this dominion. As a direct re-

146	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Thompson (Lanark)
suit of the agreements made by this government, Canada to-day has a wonderful opportunity to supply bacon to the British market. I find that in 1932 Denmark supplied 67 per cent of Great Britain's imported bacon, Poland, 10-02 per cent, Holland, 8-05 per cent, Sweden, 3-77 per cent, Lithuania, 4-52 per cent, Irish Free State, 1-75 per cent, and Canada only 1-6 per cent, the lowest percentage of any country. Under the agreement with Great Britain, Canada is permitted to send into that country 280,000,000 pounds of bacon annually. While we have doubled our exports to the British market we have not yet exceeded 25 per cent of the ' quota that has been allowed us. With pork at the price it is to-day, and still 75 per cent of our quota not taken up, there is a wonderful opportunity for the farmers of this dominion.
In the county of Lanark, which I have the honour to represent, the policies of the former government had driven our manufacturers almost to the wall. Many of our factories were closed down, few of them were running over half time. To-day every textile mill in the county of Lanark is running full time, and several are running day and night. Some of the mills that have been closed for years have been reopened. This is a direct result of the tariff policies of the present administration in restricting imports from foreign countries where the scale of wages and the standard of life is so much below that of Canada that they can afford to undersell us in our own market. The opening of these factories in Lanark county has been of great assistance to the farmers, because when the men and women engaged in industrial life have steady employment, they have purchasing power wherewith to buy the commodities that the farmers produce. Mouths are the farmers' best market.
We hear a great deal about social betterment in this country. We want social betterment, but we want it without socialism and without communism. We must have progress, in a young country like Canada we cannot stand still. Changing conditions must bring new remedies. But I have no sympathy with those organizations which would attempt to build up an economic system in Canada such as they have in Russia, based upon atheism, hatred and repudiation of debt. The danger to our present democracy does not lie in attacks made upon it by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation or similar organizations. The real danger to democracy to-day lies in the apathy of its own defenders, the men on the one hand who claim that our

present day democracy is rooted and grounded in Magna Charta and the Bill of Rights and so cannot be disturbed, and on the other hand those who use the privileges and liberties afforded by democracy to further their own selfish interests without due regard to the interests of their fellowmen. To-day we have agitation to change the whole system, but it gets us nowhere to damn it and to call it a canker on the body politic. The wise statesman must look for the cause of that eruption, and honestly- endeavour to heal it. And in lopping off the dead branches we must be careful not to destroy the living branches or the living part of the tree that has taken ages of the very best that was in humanity to produce.
Just before this house opened there was held in Ottawa a conference of the premiers of the different provinces. While the meetings were held in secret, enough has leaked out to assure the public that several of these premiers were here asking further assistance for their provinces. Now, Mr. Speaker, if these provinces have been unfortunate, if the grasshoppers have eaten them up, if the drought has burnt them out, if the hail and frost have destroyed their harvests, then I say let us come to their assistance, because these are things over which they have no control. But if those provinces insist on electing legislatures that will spend their resources unwisely, that will bonus railways, guarantee wheat pools, enter into social legislation which they cannot afford and which the application of sane business principles would have taught them to avoid, then I say it is out of the question that they can continue any such expenditure and come to Ottawa to have their bills paid.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They will not. It will not be long now.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The province of Ontario pays approximately 45 per cent of the taxes of the Dominion of Canada, Quebec approximately 30 per cent and the remainder, some 25 per cent, is paid by the other seven provinces. How long should the federal government make good-I ask as a business proposition

the extravagance of these provinces? These provinces are not poor, they have wonderful natural resources. The trouble has been poor administration. I am of the opinion that they should be told to put their own houses in order, balance their budgets, live within their means, and that it is high time they were self-sustaining. Since this government took office in 1930

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
they have had to deal with an overwhelming succession, of new phases of the economic situation for which there was no precedent in Canadian history and for which our oldest and most experienced statesmen were altogether unprepared. The fact that the ship of state has been safely guided through the dangerous shoals and is to-day heading for the high seas clearly indicates that a master hand has been at the helm.
I have every confidence in the future of this country; I am not one of those crying blue ruin. I have every confidence in the two great races that form the foundation stock of Canada, the English and the French. They have the hardihood, the business ability and the courage to surmount every obstacle that may lie in their path, and I hope they will work in unison for the future development and prosperity of our common Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):
subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is little in the
speech from the throne that is sufficiently definite to form the basis of any very clear discussion. I should like first of all, however, to protest against the military display that we witnessed at the opening. If Canada is earnestly endeavouring to promote peace it would seem to me that there is no necessity of our putting on such a warlike front. I have sometimes wondered why, at the opening of parliament, we might not have deputations of business men, of farmers, of railway men, of miners, and of those others who have laid the foundations for the life of Canada. If we had those men present instead of such a host of officials, backed up by so many military men, it would seem to me that possibly we would create an atmosphere that would bring us a little nearer reality. I suppose the practical difficulty would be that our table of precedence does not permit of anything of the kind.
The speech from the throne refers to improved world conditions. I can hardly understand this, in view of the news that is coming to us daily from almost all parts of the world. Undoubtedly we have witnessed a decline in the influence of the League of Nations; we have been witnessing the practical abandonment of the disarmament conference, and yet I take it that all thoughtful students of international affairs admit that permanent recovery is possible only as we have peace and as we are. able to develop the collective system. Further than that, we have been witnessing and participating in an intensified economic nationalism. We deprecate 74726-10$
that when it is manifested by other nations, but we have taken our full share to such an extent that from the practical point of view, it is becoming increasingly difficult, for us to market many of our primary products in Europe. We have witnessed still further in Europe the decline of many of the older democratic or so called democratic systems. There we have seen arise bolshevism, fascism and Hitlerism. Even in England there have been very radical changes, though not so much in outward form. In the United States we have had what almost might be termed a revolution, as manifested in the very great changes which the president has introduced.
In view of all these changes that are going on throughout the world I have been wondering whether there is no hope of our having a new deal for Canada. Apparently, notwithstanding the eulogistic references of the last speaker, this government is pretty much content to go along the old, beaten trail.
I think there is no member of any of the self-governing dominions who was not very decidedly perturbed by the fate of our sister dominion, Newfoundland, where they have given up even the forms of democracy. Responsible government has been replaced by administration by a commission, with what amounts to practically dictatorial powers, and I would say that this change has been made primarily not in the interests of the people of Newfoundland but in the interests of the bondholders.
The same sort of thing is going on in our western provinces and municipalities. I shall not take time to discuss the points raised by the last speaker, who referred to the extravagance of the western provinces; that would take too long. I think I could make out a case to show that we have not been more extravagant than other provinces, but the point is that at the present time we are practically bankrupt. A great many of our municipalities are actually bankrupt, and under those circumstances we cannot much longer carry on the ordinary services for which government is constituted. We face, in fact, a new type of slavery in this country, and that is bondage to the bondholders. As children we were taught that freedom had been obtained. Certain kinds of freedom have been obtained, including so called political freedom, though even that is indanger these days. But newer types of economic serfdom are being fastened upon us at the present time. I could not but recall recently a little verse by Herbert Carruth,

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
as published some years ago in Current Literature:
The rights of men are a by-word;
The bones are not yet dust
Of those who broke the shackles,
And the shackles are not yet rust [DOT]
Till the masters are forging new ones,
And coward lips are sealed
While the code that cost a million lives Is step by step repealed.
To-day we are witnessing a new type of society in which very few of us have any very large measure of freedom. I think it was Rabindranath Tagore who said some years ago that chains were none the less real because they were either invisible or golden.
I spoke of the financial condition of the municipalities and provinces of the west. Let me point out how these affect the living condition of many of our people. In the last few days in Winnipeg, my own city, we have had what might be called a doctors' strike. The doctors have refused any longer to give free medical attendance, and they have recently signed this declaration:
I undertake to refuse free medical service in the office, hospital or home to any individual in receipt of relief unless an emergency exists. An emergency is one in which life is in imminent danger and for which immediate action is required. This is to take effect on and after the 15th day of February, 1934, unless the civic and/or municipal authorities concerned have made satisfactory arrangements with our committee.
The secretary explains that even a case of ordinary confinement is not to be regarded as an emergency case, except in the case of hemorrhage or convulsions; only then will the doctor consent to come to the bedside of the patient. I do not propose to discuss the professional ethics involved in this question. I recall that some years ago when there was a strike in Winnipeg and when the milk drivers and some of the members of the fire brigades went on strike, a great cry was raised to heaven and it was said that under no circumstances should milk drivers or fire fighters desert their posts of duty. But now we have the doctors, for their own reasons, and possibly they are justifiable, in order to force an issue, refusing to give medical service to any one on relief. We all know there has been a question as to where the responsibility for giving relief lies, whether with the Dominion government or the provinces or the municipalities, and in what degree each is responsible. First of all, when we thought of relief we thought of food. Then we had to extend it to clothing, and out in our part of the world, where it is cold, we had to extend it to shelter, and even to fuel and
Xlr. Woodsworth.]
light, and as these new items have come into view we have found that it is very difficult to get agreement as to who should assume responsibility for these new types of relief.
Now we have hospitalization and medical care. I point out that owing to the practical bankruptcy of many of our municipalities it is next to impossible for them to advance further sums of money for this type of relief. The other day the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Howden), himself a medical man, raised the question in this house, and the Prime Minister's reply was that he had communicated to the representatives of the medical profession "that there was no reason to believe that the provinces would not discharge their constitutional duties with respect to the health of their citizens." Thait may be all very well, from a purely constitutional standpoint, but may I say that when there is absolute misery I cannot think that this government or any government is justified in taking such a position as that. If there was a flood, we would not stop to argue whether it was a provincial or federal responsibility to launch rafts and save the citizens; we would go out and pull out of the water the poor fellows who were threatened with being engulfed. And what then shall we say in the case of women who expect in a few days to become mothers, scores of them, who must face that very, very serious crisis in their lives with no hope of obtaining medical assistance unless their case is extreme. I think this is altogether too serious a matter to be allowed to pass unnoticed by this house. I must recall again, those words of Mr. Bennett which have been repeated very often, spoken when he was seeking to become the Prime Minister. He said:
I say to you, my fellow citizens, my fellow Canadians, speaking to the larger audience, I am convinced this problem h.as now ceased' to be local and provincial and has become national in its importance.
The Prime Minister paid a glowing tribute the other day to those to whom honours had been given, and said that some of them were doing work on the pioneer front. I want to say that if these women doing social work should be given honours, much more should help be given to those who are about to give birth to children and who have no one at the present time to look to for assistance. It is not much wonder that large numbers of them to-day are seeking to learn the principles of birth control.
The speech from the throne goes on to say that the "improved world conditions are reflected in Canada by expanding trade, im-

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
proving revenues, increasing employment, and a more confident outlook upon the future." As far as those of us from the west are concerned, that is indeed news. I am not going to enter upon the battle of figures which raged here for some hours, but I should like to call attention to some particular incidents that would seem to show that all is not just rosy at the present time.
Here is a heading and paragraph I noticed in the Toronto papers a few weeks ago, on September 26:
Machine gun tanks sent to Stratford to quiet Etrikers.	.	_
Wearing steel helmets and carrying wartime equipment the regiment detrained here this morning, prepared to guard the plant of the Swift Canadian Company and six _ furniture factories where employees are on strike.
We were told that the poultry workers were being paid two cents for each chicken plucked and that they wanted one cent more, and that it was refused them. If we are having so much prosperity it would seem to me that it might very well be reflected in the extra cent for plucking a fowl which these poultry workers asked for.
With regard to the furniture workers, they are to no small extent the victims of the mass buying recently denounced by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens). Just here I should like to suggest to the minister that we in this comer shall be very glad to cooperate in any way possible in making the investigation into that matter a success. We can assure the government of our support and will do our very best to try to uncover those bad conditions which have left so many work people, as well as the consumers, in difficulties.
But I should like to ask this. Why not also investigate the dealings of our financial promoters and manipulators? Men like Holt and others of his kind are placing burdens upon this country under which the ordinary people can hardly struggle. Only a few months ago I came across a rather interesting account of the way in which many fortunes have been made in this country. It is taken from Retrospects of a Newspaper Person, by Mr. P. D. Ross of this city. Mr. Ross had done a Mr. W. J. Carrique a good turn, and he tells in the book the interesting sequel. I quote:
Some little time further on, another visit came from Carrique. He laid an envelope on my desk. "This is your share of stock," he said. "My share? What are you talking about?" "We have formed a little company,- the Canadian Street Car Advertising Company." . . . "But, I don't want any of your stock." I said. "It won't cost you anything," returned Carrique, "It's paid-up stock." "Who paid it up?" "Nobody, It's just issued paid-up."
I opened the envelope. It contained a certificate for $10,300 paid-up stock in the Canadian Street Car Advertising Company, capital $60,000 paid up. ... "I don't know where the rest of you fellows got the money," I said. "But I haven't any money to put in this. I don't want any of it. Leave me out."
"None of us have put in any money," Carrique returned. "We have contracts for two or more years with each of the Montreal, Hamilton and Ottawa street railway companies, we to pay certain figures for _ space in their ears to place advertisements in. The agreement is to pay each company so much a month. The receipts we are already getting from advertisers to put their cards in the cars are more than enough to enable us to make our monthly payments to the street car companies1. In fact, we are already so far ahead that we could pay a dividend on $60,000 now, and we have no liabilities to anybody." "Sounds like a fairy tale, Carrique," "It's going to be a real fairy tale," he returned. "I expect the Toronto and Winnipeg franchises, and if we get them it'll be a gold mine."
Mr. Ross continues:
I took the stock. Carrique was a wonder. Before long we had the Toronto and Winnipeg franchises, with nearly all others in Canada.
Mr. Ross goes on to say that in the fifteen years following the formation of the company he had drawn in dividends or bonuses the sum of $78,847, and the account continues:
No shareholder ever paid a dollar-not a cent-into the company. In 1919, W. J. Carrique, who was a shrewd and successful operator in other things than street railway advertising, died a near-millionaire. The Carrique estate and the rest of us soon after sold the total stock of the Canadian Street. Railway Advertising Company to Senator-Wilson of Montreal for $337,500. My share-of the proceeds of the sale was a cheque for $58,185. This, with the $78,847 received during the previous years in dividends, constituted a total of $127,032 which came to me in fifteen years from the Canadian Street Railway Advertising Company from stock for which I never put up a cent-never anything except a small amount of obligingness.
Can one wonder that Mr. Ross entitled that chapter " Why not be Obliging?" I do not know whether that is the kind of fortune that the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) would say was earned by honest toil.
There is another strike to which I should like to refer, that of the lumberworkers in northern Ontario and the Rouyn district of Quebec. Harsh and repressive measures were used, yet according to the Montreal Star of January 4, the provincial government's own investigators-
All agree that the workers are being exploited by a number of contractors and sub-contractors, that their wages are inadequate, and that the goods sold to the workers in the stores operated by contractors are exorbitantly priced, so that when the season is over_ the lumberjacks find themselves not any richer

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
than before and sometimes poorer, for they are indebted to their employers for part of the goods purchased.
I should like to ask again: Why not some sort of labour code for Canada? If any of the workers in Canada have been better off in the last year it has been as a reflection of the action taken by the American government. I think that is true, for example, of the shingle-weavers on the Pacific coast.
What is this government doing? The Prime Minister declared recently in Vancouver that this government would not be a wet nurse for derelicts. The public was shocked when it realized the large number of unemployed and their plight. The Prime Minister explained in a later speech that he was speaking of derelict industries. On that basis I should like to ask about the textile industry which has been helped for many years by this and other governments. I should like to ask about the $60,000,000 guaranteed to the Canadian Pacific Railway. Is that not being a wet nurse to a derelict enterprise? That is what it seems to me to be. Hundreds of small concerns have been in dire straits and many of them have gone under but yet we find that in the case of a large concern the government comes to its aid. It is all very well to conserve the interests of the shareholders of the Canadian Pacific Railway located in Canada, Great Britain, the United States or elsewhere, but if that is to be done I submit that the interests of those engaged in smaller industries in Canada have an equal right to be taken care of. The only consolation I get out of the transaction is that it is a step towards public ownership. I should like to make a practical suggestion. If we are to guarantee $60,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific Railway, this house ought to know whether the salary of Mr. Beatty has been cut by ten or twenty per cent. If we are to guarantee, we ought to know something about the inside history of the company. If we are to pay the debts, we ought to have something to say as to what the expenditures will be.'A
The government has recently recommended certain titles and honours but I do not intend to take up very much time in the discussion of this matter. Two more people can boast of titles because of Mr. Bennett having been Prime Minister. But hundreds of people have lost the titles which they had to their property. Most people are more interested in having a title to their little home than in having a title which may be recognized in the old country. In referring to the royal prerogative the other day it seems to me that the Prime Minister was talking a lot of solemn non-

sense. As a matter of fact by insisting upon making the exercise of the royal prerogative dependent upon an act of parliament, the Prime Minister is in reality degrading the royal prerogative. I should like to come to its defence. Let me quote from page 409 of the sixth edition of The Law of the Constitution by A. V. Dicey, as follows:
The survival of the prerogative, conferring as it does wide discretionary authority upon the cabinet, involves a consequence which constantly escapes attention. It immensely increases the authority of the House of Commons, and ultimately of the constituencies by which that house is returned. Ministers must in the exercise of all discretionary powers inevitably obey the predominant authority in the state. When the King was the chief member of the sovereign body, ministers were in fact no less than in name the King's servants. At periods of our history when the peers were the most influential body in the country, the conduct of the ministry represented with more or less fidelity the wishes of the peerage. Now that the House of Commons has become by far the most important part of the sovereign body, the ministry in all matters of discretion carry out, or tend to carry out, the will of the house. When however the cabinet cannot act except by means of legislation, other considerations come into play. A law- requires the sanction of the House of Lords. No government can increase its statutory authority without obtaining the sanction of the upper chamber.
If I understand the Prime Minister aright, he seemed to want to make any limitation of the exercise of the royal prerogative in Canada with regard to titles dependent upon the action of parliament, the Commons, the Senate and the Governor General. Let me quote one further paragraph from Dicey, as follows:
The prerogatives of the crown have become the privileges of the pepole, and anyone who wants to see how widely these privileges may conceivably be stretched as the House of Commons becomes more and more the direct representative of the true sovereign, should u-eigh well the words in which Bagehot describes the powers which can still legally be exercised by the crow-n without consulting parliament; and should remember that these powers can now be exercised by a cabinet who are really servants, not of the crown, but of a representative chamber which in turn obeys the behests of the electors.
We had a flaunting of the authority of this house the other day when the Prime Minister went back one hundred years for his authority. In that time the Commons has acquired a new' status. I quote Bagehot as follows:
I said in this book that it would very much surprise people if they were only told how-many things the Queen could do without consulting parliament, and it certainly has so proved, for when the Queen abolished purchase in the army by an act of prerogative (after the Lords had rejected the bill for doing so), there was a great and general astonishment.

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
But this is nothing to what the Queen can by law do without consulting parliament. Not to mention other things, she could disband the army (by law she cannot engage more than a certain number of men, but she is not obliged to engage any men); she could dismiss all the officers, from the general commanding-in-chief downwards; she could dismiss all the sailors too; she could sell off all our ships-of-war and all our naval stores; she could make a peace by the sacrifice of Cornwall, and begin a war for the conquest of Brittany. She could make every citizen in the United Kingdom, male or female, a peer; she could make every parish in the United Kingdom a "university"; she could dismiss most of the civil servants; she could pardon all offenders. In a word, the Queen could by prerogative upset all the action of civil government within the government, could disgrace the nation by a bad war or peace, and could, by disbanding our forces, whether land or sea, leave us defenceless against foreign nations.
The Prime Minister proved altogether too much. Let me quote another paragraph from Dicey, as follows;
If government by parliament is ever transformed into government by the House of Commons, the transformation will, it may be conjectured, be effected by use of the prerogatives of the crown.
The speech refers to certain industries which were flourishing in this country. I think of two, gold and nickel. Roosevelt is to-day taking over ail coined gold supply, and I should like to ask this question: Why should Canada continue to pay premiums for gold mined in Canada? It has always been a mystery to me. Further, what is going to be the effect on gold in this country of the decision of the American government to devaluate the dollar? If the gold content of the American dollar is to be altered, who is going to benefit in Canada-the same American corporations which all along have been benefiting? If gold is so essential, why should not gold mining become a public work for the general advantage of Canada? I suggested several years ago that we should establish work camps in the gold mining areas for the unemployed and pay them, decent wages, allowing the profits to go to the government and not to American corporations.
Another industry that seems to have been prospering is nickel. Undoubtedly a large proportion of the nickel mined in this country is destined ultimately for the manufacture of war munitions; I do not think anyone can seriously question that. " We in Canada very easily protest against the private manufacture of armaments, but in this country we have almost a monopoly of nickel; and nickel it seems, under present processes, is essential to the manufacture of armaments. Well then,
if we are really serious in our wish for peace, why should we permit the unregulated export of nickel destined to build up armaments in Europe? I would urge that the government seriously consider taking over control of the export of nickel, or better still, that they make nickel mining a government monopoly. It seems to me that if we have any difficulty at all in tracing the ultimate destination of nickel, we might readily call in the good offices of the League of Nations and at least block this one avenue to the manufacture of armaments.
The speech announces that we are to have public works. I am very glad of that, although I hope it will not be thought ungracious if I say that in my opinion we ought to have had such a program two or three years ago. I would suggest however that when these works are put into operation the workers engaged therein be given decent wages and not merely doles.
I am glad also that a central bank is to be established. We shall have an opportunity to discuss this question at greater length later on. But let me say at the outset that we in this comer will do our utmost to insist that it shall not be a privately-owned or controlled institution. Incidentally, I wonder whether the banking commission, however admirable its report, was absolutely necessary. The Prime Minister recently revealed to the Western Ontario Conservative association that over two years ago he had decided on a central bank. If it had been decided upon before the commission was appointed, possibly we might have saved the expenses of that commission.
There is one rather curious omission from the speech, and that is the usual reference to this season's bountiful harvest. I think perhaps it might have been almost fitting if there had been an expression of gratitude to the drought and grasshoppers that came to the help of the government. I am not among those who say that there should be no control of production; as a believer in planned economy, I think that control of production will have to come. But I think the government is getting at the problem from the wrong end. The Prime Minister suggests that there must be a balance between production and consumption, and that we must therefore limit production. I think we ought to have a try at expanding consumption, because there are undoubtedly large numbers of consumers the world over who cannot obtain access to the supplies of wheat which they might readily use, and if there is to be an international policy to reduce production,

The Address-Mr. Woodsworth
surely it should be possible to have some sort of international policy to increase consumption. If we are to have a reduction in production it will prove disastrous unless accompanied by other measures; I think we shall have to have other measures as well.
The Prime Minister the other day spoke of being guided by business interests. I am not at all sure that the business men are convinced that this reduction in production is a very good thing. On October 12, addressing a public gathering at Saskatoon, the Prime Minister said: "Would you not rather have one bushel of wheat you can sell for a dollar than two bushels you cannot sell for fifty cents?" Everyone will agree to that proposition. But there is no guarantee in the agreement either that the farmers will be able to sell or that they will be able to get a price. An editorial in Canadian Business, published by the Canadian Chambers of Commerce, and appearing in October, put the matter thus:
The government has guaranteed to limit exports to 200 million bushels, but in return has not received any guarantee for the sale of that or even a lesser quantity. It is also claimed that with the quantities of wheat available there is little likelihood of prices reaching, in the near future, at any rate, a figure necessitating a fulfilment of the tariff revision obligations of the importing countries.
I was very much interested in the comment of the Free Press, which is not exactly favourable to reduction. The Free Press of January 20, 1934, admits that:
-the Alberta farmers have an air-tight case. ... If the Canadian government proposes to make itself responsible for the quantity of wheat grown and sold in the dominion, it must guarantee an income to the farmers, whose right to compete freely as producer and seller it abridges.
These, I think, are some of the other measures that will have to be enacted supplementary to the control of production.

There is a reference to it. The speech announces another loan. That is a still heavier mortgage on Canada. The public debt of Canada, includ-
[Mr. Woodsworth.!
ing federal, provincial, municipal debts and those of public corporations, amounts now to $8,652,727,000. These figures are taken from the report of the Royal Commission on Banking. Our population is a little over ten millions, and this means $800 per head. At 5 per cent it would represent $40 a year interest per head of population. If we take the average family of five, that would mean $200 a year that we have to pay in interest charges on the public debt. This is an appalling amount and I should like to suggest that whether the present government or the official opposition is in power, to say nothing of our group ever being in power, that money will not ultimately be paid; it cannot be paid. On New Year's Day I remember on the front page of one of our city papers there appeared a photograph of twin babies born on that day. I would like to have a cartoon made and to hang around the neck of each of those two babies a little tag bearing the words "Eight hundred dollars mortgage." Those two children started out in life on New Year's Day, each mortgaged with S800 of public debt, to say nothing of the over-capitalized industrial debt which bears so heavily on each one of us in this country.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They might have the $800 coming to them.

They might have.
There is that much in resources, but it is not available.
I am glad to say that one of the new members recognizes the problem; the new member for Mackenzie (Mr. MacMillan) according to a dispatch by Mr. Hart to the Winnipeg Free Press of October 13 last, said:
Conscription of wealth to wipe out Canada's burden of debt was advocated by J. A. MacMillan, Liberal Candidate in Mackenzie riding, while speaking at a public meeting held here Thursday night.
He gave figures with regard to this heavy debt and then went on to say:
I am not an extremist, hut I believe that the same authority that came into our homes during the war and took our sons from the knees of their mothers, because there was a national emergency, should not he afraid to take similar steps to bring to the aid of the nation all surplus wealth. We conscripted men, why not money? There is now another national emergency that will have to be faced resolutely and squarely, if the country is to weather the storm. One of the ways out of the difficulty would be to get rid of the terrible burden of interest by paying off a substantial portion of the national debt, and this can only be done by conscription of wealth.
I welcome that statement from the new member for Mackenzie, but I should like to ask: Does the leader of the opposition (Mr-

The Address-Mr. Marcil
Mackenzie King) agree? The Liberal party rather puzzles me. Only a few months ago the Hon. Vincent Massey, president of the National Liberal Federation, speaking at Lake Couchiching conference on The New Economic Nationalism, said:
It's a difficult world to live in; we are witnessing the very transition between old' laissez-faire improvising ways of doing things, and a tightly planned modern state system. We have to plan our own recovery in this easy-going country of ours, our own reconstruction, our own relationship to this new world.
And again:
The primary conflict is not therefore isolation versus internationalism but planning versus improvisation, and in this trouble planning will, I believe, be victorious.
Once again:
It must suffice for me to say that national planning will have to be the foundation of Canada's international relations. Old conceptions of government must give place to new.
Needless to say, I heartily agree, but I ask: Does the leader of the opposition agree? That is the question?

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry that the forty minute rule which applies to the ordinary member deprives me of the pleasure of following the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) over the ground which he has covered, as I had already prepared some notes on which I desire to speak referring to the portion of the country which I represent. Opportunity, however, may be given us later on in the session to refer to some of the points raised by the hon. member who lately has laid before the country a new policy which has startled many parts of it and has not been accepted as thoroughly, freely or quickly as probably he had expected.
The old custom that was in existence when I first came into the house, I see, still prevails, of congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address. A couple of days ago the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) came over to my desk to remind me that he and I had had the honour of sitting in parliament for thirty-eight sessions. This is our thirty-eighth session. We are the sole survivors of the parliament of 1900, and looking over the Parliamentary Companion some time ago I was amazed to note that 1,080 members have gone through parliament since the Minister of Justice and I had the honour of being elected for the first time, he for South Wellington and I for Bonaventure. He moved the address and
I had the honour of seconding his motion. I am glad Providence has been kind to us that we have both been able to pass through all this turmoil and stress through which Canada has passed during the last thirty-four years we have been here and in which period thirty-eight sessions have been held. I congratulate the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil) who, as an active young man, came into parliament last election, and the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) on the way in which they accomplished the difficult task which they had to perform. Moving and seconding the address is not always as pleasant a duty as it might be, but in their case they acquitted themselves well in what was a hard task to perform. .
Reading over the speech from the throne and looking back to the program of the present government and its actions since it came into power in 1930, I recalled the first election in which I took part officially. The famous election of 1878 which terminated on September 17, and by which honest Alexander Mackenzie was beaten at the polls on the so-called national policy. I had the honour on that day of being returning officer and representative to a certain extent of Hon. Mr. Mcrcier who ran in the county of St. Hyacinthe and was defeated by the present Judge Tellier, now dean of the Quebec bench, a retired judge, on the great question of the national policy when Canada went back on the tariff for revenue and took up Sir John A. Macdonald and his colleagues after their escapade of the Canadian Pacific railway scandal, entrusting them again with the government of this country under the old banner of protection and high tariff. I have no time to go back to what protection did or to what was called then an infant Industry. When Sir John A. Macdonald delivered his speech in the house he started to qualify this protection as being intended for the infant industry. Canada was then a different country from what it is to-day. A long time has elapsed since then. Our population has increased; our revenue has increased; our standing in the eyes of the world is vastly different, but our liabilities, responsibilities and the burdens which we have to carry have also greatly increased.
When Sir John A. Macdonald, great statesman that he was, appealed to the Canadian nation for support on hiis policy, he appealed to them naturally with what at the time was the most pressing appeal that could be made.
The Address-Mr. Marcil

There was unemployment in the country. He promised to give the people employment, to open factories, to give Canadians the control of the Canadian market, he promised to bring back prosperity to Canada. Alexander Mackenzie had refused to raise the low tariff we had then for revenue purposes, because he thought the manufacturers of Canada were well enough protected at that time and that it was not fair to bleed the consumer for the benefit of the manufacturer, so rather than go into this new adventure of protection and higher tariffs that Sir John took up Mackenzie was beaten at the polls. Sir John took up protection, and we had protection with a vengeance, although nothing compared with that of 1930. It was a boon for the infant industries, they grew, and the Liberal party complained year after year that this protection, instead of being reduced as the infant industries grew, continued to increase. Then in 1896 the blast came. Canada was on the rocks. Protection in Canada was as dead as a doornail. The Canadian west was almost given up, the Canadian Pacific was running its trains with no revenue, Canada in fact was in a retrograde position. That was the effect of protection after its trial from 1878 to 1896.
Then we had the Liberal boom. Why had we that Liberal boom? Because Laurier opened the doors to our trade; Laurier, with Fielding, brought about the British preference, and Canada boomed. In 1911 I had the honour of occupying your chair, Mr. Speaker, and I remember as well as though it were yesterday, when Fielding and Paterson offered the Reciprocity treaty to this house. The only thing that- could 'be said against it was that it was a dangerous thing to deal with Americans, and that Canada was doing well enough alone, and matters Should be left as they were.
In 1911 the Reciprocity treaty was turned down. But there is no man in Canada today who knows conditions and is willing to be frank but will admit that Canada committed a grievous mistake at that time. When the right hon. Prime Minister, whose talents no one would deny, whose devotion to his party, and I hope to his country, is unquestioned, took up the leadership of the Conservative party I looked back to the days of Sir John A. Macdonald to see how the programs compared. I realized that he was making the same appeal that Sir John had made in 1878: "I will give you the Canadian market,
I will make Canadians masters of their own market"! He did that, but since Canadians 
have been masters of their own market Canadians have no money to buy the products produced in Canada. The present Prime Minister repeated Sir John A. Macdonald's program, took up the same cry, and with the same result; he secured office. The people trusted to what he said, every man is anxious to get a job when he is out of work, every manufacturer desires to get a market if the market he has is not satisfactory. But the failure that came to Sir John's policy has come much more quickly to the policy of the present Prime Minister, because conditions have changed from what they were in 1878. Communications to-day are different, countries are linked together by rail, water and air, the telegraph and the radio. Such was not the case in 1878. When I heard the Prime Minister in 1930 move these high tariffs, my mind wandered back to the days when Wilfrid Laurier and Alexander Mackenzie and Richard Cartwright and Mills and Davis and Fielding and Blair and all those stalwarts of the Liberal party fought day and night against such policies as being suicidal to Canada. High tariffs will never suit Canada, with its immense resources, its enormous territory and its great future. The mistake the Prime Minister made in bringing about this new policy of his had been committed in the United States by the Republican party. The Republican party had closed the doors and raised the walls against other countries, and wanted to subsist to themselves. What was the result? When Hoover appealed to the people last March he faced an army of 14,000,000 unemployed out of a population of 120,000,000. When the Prime Minister went to the country lie knew there were 100,000 unemployed in Canada. How many are there to-day? How many were there last year? I am willing to admit that if the Liberal party had been in office during the last three years with the same policy that our friends now have in force we would have had the same results. But if the Liberal party had been in power we would not have had that policy. We would not have closed the doors, we would have continued to do business as we had in the past. The leader of the opposition gave figures; I have no time to refer to figures, but our trade has dropped $2,000,000 a day since the present administration has been in office. Is it any wonder there is hardship in this country.
I represent one of ithe oldest) parts of Canada. It was on the point of Gospe, four hundred years ago next July, that Jacques Cartaer landed in North America and took

The Address-Mr. Marcil
possession of this northern part of it in the name of the Icing of France, and erected thereon the cross of civilization. That was the discovery of Canada, and I hope the present government will see to it that the four hundredth anniversary of this great event in the history of this country is properly commemorated. I know representations have already been made to the government. Dates such as this should not be forgotten and should not be allowed to pass unnoticed.
I have had the honour of representing the county of Gaspe for thirty-four years out of the forty-two years it has given its allegiance to the Liberal party. I declare that never have I known conditions to exist in the Gaspe peninsula such as have existed during the last two or three years. When I went down there last year we had been talking about controlling the production of wheat in western Canada, but there were families of poor fishermen on the Gaspe coast who had no bread to eat. Some have no bread this winter, they are subsisting on fish and potatoes-when they can get them. They have no work; our lumber industry is dead, our shanties closed, our mills idle, our fish selling ait one or two cents a pound. We have no markets of any kind. We talk about central banks, talk about the control of currency, talk about the amalgamation of railways, talk about all these hundred questions that come before us, but what is the cause of all our trouble? The cause is that we have no markets for what we produce and the policy of this government has made us lose what markets we had. That is the cause of the whole trouble. Find a market for what the farmer produces, for what the fisherman produces, for the product of the miner and the lumberman, and your troubles are solved.
When the Prime Minister came into this house in 1911 I had been here eleven years before that time. He came with wild denunciations of reciprocity with the United States. Is there anything more foolish than to condemn such a policy? Are we not destined forever to have dealings with our great neighbour? The great natural market of this country ds the United States. As the United States prospers so will Canada prosper, and as long as the United States does not prosper no prosperity is possible to this country. I am a British subject, I was bom a British subject, and in the words of one of my great countrymen, I shall die a British subject. But never forget, Mr. Speaker, that in matters of trade we are talking business and not of political allegiance. Whatever our
business may be with the British Empire and the sister dominions it will be always infinitesimal compared to what it should be, what it might be and what it ought to be with the United States of America. Give us the American market to-day; give us the market Laurier, Fielding and Paterson obtained, and immediately you annex 120,000,000 people to this country. My hon. friend from Manitoba who has sait here with me for many years is interested in live stock. Give him the American market and see what will become of the live stock business.

speechtext: Hogs?

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Yes, anything; give us the American market and you will see that Canada will change overnight.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You lost it, not we.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Sir Wilfrid Laurier went down in 1911, but thank God he went down fighting for a good cause. He fell fighting for the noblest cause ever advanced in this country. Even now, Mr. Speaker, to his eternal memory let it be said that his name is never mentioned in this house except by way of eulogy and in defence of the great principles which he initiated and brought before the Canadian people.
The cause for which Sir Wilfrid Laurier fell is just as important to-day as it was then. How can Canada prosper if the United States does not prosper? How can Canada hope to get along without the United States? Down in my constituency we have no markets for our fish, our lumber or our agricultural products. Thousands of our men are unemployed; they write to me every day and say, "Marcil, you are an old member of parliament. Is there no means by which you can bring about an appeal to the people so that we can have an election and change the political system of Canada? The present system is ruining us. We cannot stand it any longer. We have no work and nothing to eat." When I went to my constituency last summer the first man I met said, "Can't you give me a chance to earn a dollar? I have not seen a dollar for a year." What I say is absolutely true; if the government doubt it let them bring on a by-election in Bona-venture county or in any part of Canada and they will find out that I am correct.
I should like to correct a mistake which the Prime Minister inadvertently made the other day. The constituency of Restigouche-Madawaska adjoins my constituency; we are only separated by the Restigouehe river. The right hon. gentleman said that Restigouche-Madawaska had not elected a Conservative
The Address-Mr. Marcil

since 1896, blit that was a slip. In 1925 Mr. Culligan defeated Mr. Michaud in that constituency, and in 1930 Mi. Cormier was elected, so that from 1896 until 1930, in five elections there were three Liberals and two Conservatives returned. Apparently that is good fighting ground. But here is a remarkable fact. This county, which in 1930 elected a Conservative by a majority of five hundred, turned around and defeated the candidate of the same party by a majority of six thousand, and the Conservative candidate lost his deposit. The candidate of the party led by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) was defeated just as badly. The Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) came into my county last summer and warned the people against the coalition that was being formed between the C.C.F. and the Liberals. I am sorry the Solicitor General is not here; of course he was not sincere in what he said, but he warned the good people of Bonaventure not to vote Liberal because the Liberal party were working hand in hand with the C.C.F. The result was quite unexpected, of course.
There are other matters to which I should like to refer, Mr. Speaker, with regard to my constituency. No doubt in the last few days the Minister of Railways (Mr. Manion) has noticed that the eastern part of Canada has suffered from the most severe snowstorms in its history. They say that such a condition has not prevailed in the eastern part of Quebec and the maritime provinces for twenty-five years. No less than four of the. crack trains of the Canadian National railways were tied up at one time by snow in the Matapedia valley, a large part of which is in my constituency. Of course I am not blaming the government for this.

speechtext:
It is the only thing we
have not been blamed for.

subsubtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Snow is the only thing we
have in abundance down there, and that abundance comes from providence. There is something that could be done by the Department of Railways, however. The minister is always very pleasant and agreeable, and judging from the number of speeches which he has to deliver all over the country-and his speeches are always interesting and entertaining-he is one of the most popular members of the administration. During the recess I followed his advice and arranged a meeting with Mr. Appleton, the manager of the eastern lines of the Canadian National railways, at Matapedia.
Here are the circumstances, Mr. Speaker. When we took over the Gaspe railway the

people of the province of Quebec, who had built this railway as a provincial line, expected that it would remain part and parcel of the Quebec system of railways. We had the terminal at Matapedia, which was the connecting point between the Gaspe railway and the Canadian National railways. When this railway was taken over the late Sir Henry Thornton promised us that he would give it a fair trial, and he left the terminal at Matapedia. Shortly after his sad departure, however, the terminal was changed overnight to Campbellton. So we have a train that runs two hundred miles through the Gaspe basin to Matapedia; then it goes back thirteen miles to Campbellton, over the ground that it covered an hour before, to hand over the mail and deliver passengers. The only alternative is to leave the other passengers stranded on the platform at Matapedia until the train comes back again.
All the chambers of commerce in the province of Quebec, the commercial travellers' association, the Solicitor General and God knows who else have protested. There has been a war on for a year past between the Post Office Department and the railway administration with regard to the cost of carrying these mails from Matapedia to Campbellton and back again. I am told that it cost the Post Office Department $2,000 extra last year to carry these mails down and back. The Postmaster General has been appealed to, as have the Solicitor General and the Minister of Marine, who represent the province of Quebec. Now I want to lay my case before the Minister of Railways. No doubt he will tell me that he has nothing to do with the matter, but that will not work with the people. I know the minister is a friend of the railway-men; his candidate in Restigouche-Mada-waska was a railway man, but now the people of Matapedia want this question settled.*
We all know that Mr. Hungerford, who is an experienced railway man of high standing, has been promoted-and fairly, I think-to the position of president of the Canadian National railways. He should view this question as it ought to be viewed. Here is the oldest province in the Dominion of Canada, a province which, with Ontario, carries about three-quarters of the burden of this country. We built this railway; we were given poor service for many years. Now we have an improved service, and we want to keep what properly belongs to us. Why should the terminal be moved from Matapedia to Campbellton, thirteen miles out of the way in New Brunswick? They say it was done because of economy. When Mr. Appleton attended a public meeting in Matapedia he wanted us to

The Address-Mr. Marcil
appeal to the Board of Railway Commissioners, but how can you expect a lot of poor people in a village down in Bonaventure to undertake to fight the Canadian National railways and prove that it is cheaper to run trains to Matapedia than to Campbellton? We asked the railway commission if they would not inquire into the matter, and they said: No, we cannot unless we get an appeal to us. The people of the district would not appeal because they say that once a decision is rendered it will never be reversed. I ask the Minister of Railways to take that matter up and do justice to the people of that district. Here are people who have had a terminus in their village for the last forty years. It is taken away without any cause or reason, without any benefit or advantage, and at great trouble and greater cost. Why should that condition of affairs continue to prevail?
I hope the Minister of Railways will change it.
They talk of economy on the railways, Mr. Speaker. Last December there was an unfortunate accident in my county on the Canadian National railway. An engine driver, John Allard, who had been in the service of the road for forty years, was taking his train through a snow storm, his engine being coupled to the snowplough in .front of it. His engine was hauling a long train, and when the snowplough came to the trestle at St. Charles de Caplan the snowplough toppled over and fell into the Bale des Chaleurs, bringing the locomotive and tender down with it. Poor John Allard lost his life. Fortunately the link between the tender and the passenger cars broke and the train remained on the track; but if that had not happened, instead of one life being lost, one hundred lives might have been lost. I am told that this was contrary to railway practice. Is it customary to couple these snowploughs to passenger trains? Is it not rather the practice to send out the snowplough followed by a caboose to clear the track? If the practice that resulted in the loss of this man's life is allowed to prevail on the Gaspe railway, where bridges have to be crossed over the river almost every ten miles, and bridges with difficult approaches, sharp curves and so on, such an accident is likely to happen again. If these snowploughs have to be sent forward before the passenger train comes along, let them be sent with a caboose, and not placed ahead of the passenger train.

May I say to my hon.
friend that to-morrow I shall very gladly send a copy of his speech to Mr. Justice Fullerton, the chairman of the board of trustees, and ask him to give the matter every consideration.
Of course, my hon. friend knows that I have no control whatsoever in either of these matters that he has brought up.

I agree, but the position
I take is this: When parliament speaks it speaks for all, and when I first came to this house, a member of parliament was somebody and a minister was somebody. When I saw Laurier or Blair or some other minister, what I said for my county was the law, and I was held responsible by the minister for what was done in my constituency, and the trust was well reposed, I think, because the people have held me there for thirty-four years. But now they say: Marcil, you are an older man; you are not as smart as you used to be.
I tell them that conditions have changed.
Talk about Mr. Justice Fullerton-there is just one instance of the change that has taken place. Parliament has abdicated its functions in respect of the railways into the hands of Judge Fullerton. Llis salary has not been cut. I must congratulate him upon that. His salary was raised-

His personal salary was
not cut, but the salary, and allowances, of Sir Henry Thornton was higher than his by $125,000.'

speechtext:
Sir Henry Thornton is
dead and the other man is alive. There is another instance,, Mr. Speaker, of what parliament has been doing. When you talk to the common people of railway commissions, board of railway commissioners, tariff commissions, soldiers' commissions, land commissions, and so on, they say:	What is the use
of your going to Ottawa? My reply is, Well, I am going there merely to vote the money that is necessary to carry on these commissions. As a matter of fact, we have abdicated all of our powers. We have no power at all. Parliament to-day is administered by order in council. There is a notice on the order paper to-day by the Prime Minister, who is going to have an inquiry into the spread between producer and consumer. The hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil), who moved the address in reply, talked about New Zealand butter. He was elected on New Zealand butter. Canadian butter at the time of his election was selling at thirty cents, but last year in my constituency the farmers got nine cents for their butter, and they are * dying now for an opportunity to vote the other way. The quality of that butter selling at nine cents a pound is firSt-class because I may say that the butter of the parish of Bonaventure took first prize for the province of Quebec.
The Address-Mr. Marcil

speechtext: On the market it is selling at from twenty to twenty-two cents. That is what we pay for it here.

speechtext: That is not an answer to my question. I asked if the hon. member knew the average price for butter in 1933?
