speechtext:
I am telling you what my
farmers get for their butter in Bonaventure, and it is about nine cents a pound, and if the hon. gentleman wants to know their feeling in the matter he might go down there and consult them and see what they think about it.
In the time left at my disposal I am unable to refer to the speech from the throne at any great length, except to say this:	My
conception of the duty of the government is to try to undo what was done in 1930. In 1930, in order to carry out the promises which they had made in the election campaign, something had to be done, and the government said: We will raise the tariff. They tried to make the people believe that Canadian trade would expand under their policy and that the number of the unemployed would be decreased. That policy has been a dead failure, Mr. Speaker.
As I said a moment ago, the first election I took part in was on September 17, 1878.
I have been in public life for over fifty years, and I may say that in the thirty-four years I have been in this parliament, never has a Canadian government made such a terrible fiasco as the present government. It is not because of want of clever men, because there are many clever men in the cabinet. Right opposite me, for instance, sits the former premier of Nova Scotia, and I see also my old friend the Minister of Justice, as well as many other clever men. The fiasco is due to a wrong policy-this wrong policy of hemming Canada in with high tariff walls. We are spending $250,000 on the League of Nations every year, and what has the league been telling us all the time? They have said that these high tariffs, these trade barriers, promote economic war, and that economic war leads to military war. Why are we squandering money in sending representatives to the League of Nations and then going contrary to its recommendations?
I want to congratulate the leader of the opposition on the speech he made on the League of Nations and on his magnificent speech in this house the other day which it 
took four hours on the part of the Prime Minister to try to demolish. I say, Mr. Speaker, that this tariff policy of Canada must be changed. We must lower our tariffs and open our gates to the outside world as a whole. We must have relations not only with the British Empire but with the whole world. We must have relations with the United States of America, which is our greatest neighbour.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) tells us that each of us carries a mortgage of $800 around his neck. This government does not want to deal with the Americans, but it is ready enough to enter into a treaty with them to give over our greatest heritage, the greatest asset that Canada possesses, that system of waterways in the St. Lawrence and the great lakes. This government wants to go into partnership with the Americans to. bring about the development of waterpower and navigation. There is no sane man in this country who ever navigated salt water-I am sorry the hon. member for Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) is not present at the moment- who will tell you that any ocean-going steamer will ever go up beyond Montreal. It is true that small steamers may go as far as Duluth. When Jacques Cartier and Maisonneuve selected Montreal as the head of navigation, they were wise in their day. Beyond that point you can have lake and river navigation, but the large ocean-going steamers will stop at Montreal. Nothing goes beyond Montreal. The tendency is towards the building of larger ships and at the present time many ships cannot go beyond Quebec. Why should we enter into a treaty of this kind at a time when we have no money to meet our engagements and when not only the dominion but the provinces are weighed down with burdens. I heard the Prime Minister state the other day that we had spent $141,000,000 in helping the provinces give relief to the unemployed. I can remember the days when this country had a budget not as large as that. The city of Ottawa has 6,000 families on relief. Practically under the Peace Tower which honours this building we have a refuge which has been running day and night for the last three years. Hundreds of thousands of people out of work have been fed here and the same thing applies all over the dominion. Is that not enough to open the eyes of any man who has a desire to see what is going on?
We must reverse our policy and the sooner we do it the better. If the Prime Minister wants to know what is the feeling of the country, let him go before the people. In

The Address-Mr. Marcil
all the years I have sat in this chamber it has always been customary for a government to go to the people at the end of four years, but the Prime Minister has had five sessions. There was only one other government that committed the mistake of not going to the people at the end of four years. That was the Tapper government of 1896. They had six sessions and hon. members know what happened to them-they were put out of office.' We must reverse our policy as soon as possible. We should have a tariff for revenue purposes only. We should carry on the policies that Laurier and Fielding delegated to us when they left public life.
Hon. members should remember the position which Canada occupied in 1911 and compare it with our present position. In those days the St. Lawrence had been transformed into one of the great waterways of the world. Hon. members will remember the map of the British Empire which was printed in red upon the stamp which that grand old man of Ontario, Sir William Muloek, had accepted by this house. I cannot mention that name without recalling that out of that first government which I had the honour of supporting there are to-day but two survivors, Sir William Muloek and Sir Charles Fitzpatrick, the former Lieutenant Governor of Quebec. These men did something for Canada. They placed Canada on the map. They had a policy which was acceptable to other nations. When Laurier shared with Queen Victoria the honours of the Jubilee in London and when She pressed upon him the acceptance of the title which had been conferred, Canada had entered upon the great golden era which extended from 1896 to 1911. We had free markets and free intercourse with other nations except for purposes of revenue.
We cannot impose high tariffs without their being beneficial to someone. If they are beneficial to the government, they are not beneficial to the consumer. If they are not beneficial to the government, they are not beneficial to anyone. A tariff is nothing but a tax. If revenues are falling, as they are to-day, what is the reason? It is because the tariff is too high and therefore there are no importations. When there are no importations, there is no revenue, and when there is no revenue, then we must borrow and keep on borrowing. We go to London and float a loan for S75,000,000. Is there any country in the world that would refuse to lend money to Canada? Canada is one of the most promising countries in the world. We occupy the best part of the North American com tinent and we can pay all that we borrow.
The hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson) mentioned immigration. I remember when his predecessors John Haggart, Sir John A. Macdonald and others contended that the future of this country rested upon the immigration policy of the Conservative party. They endeavoured to bring immigrants to this country but they had not the Canada which Laurier made. They had not a cheap country in which to live. When Laurier went out of office he had succeeded in creating two new provinces in the west, Alberta and Saskatchewan. As Deputy Speaker of this house I had the honour of signing the bills creating those new provinces. Laurier put over a million new people into the west. These were consumers and they are the mainstay of the -west to-day. Our right hon. friend represents Calgary, but what was Calgary in those days? What were Edmonton and Winnipeg? The west was a wilderness except for the narrow strip of the Canadian Pacific Railway. Laurier developed the west along with Sifton who was in charge of the immigration policy. They brought a million strangers into the west and those people are represented to-day in this house. The fathers of some of our present members were numbered among the newcomers of those days. Is there anyone who will say that we have not room for 25,000,000 or 50,000,000 people? If the country on the other side of the line can harbour 120,000.000 with practically the same territory, why should we be content with only 10,000,000? But we have reached this point: instead of expanding and developing, instead of going towards the future with buoyant revenues and buoyant trade and a cheerful population, we are oppressed and weighed down, Our people are dissatisfied and discontented. Policies are being carried out which were never heard of in the days of Macdonald or Laurier. Canada has been changed because of a false fiscal policy.
I believe in the sincerity and optimism of my fellow members on the other side but I reiterate what I have always said, their present policy is a false policy. That fact was decided by Sir John A. Macdonald, the greatest Roman of them all, and when his great successor, Sir Charles Tupper, came into office in 1896, the national policy of those days was as dead as a doornail. That was replaced with the policy of Fielding and Laurier, a policy of reciprocity with the British Empire and with the United States and-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to continue the debate on the address let me at the outset extend my congratulations to the mover (Mr. Gobeil) and the seconder (Mr. Barber) of the address. I think we all appreciate the fact that the task assigned to these two hon. members was not an easy one. I think we all agree that they endeavoured to present the views of the government in a clear, moderate and forceful manner and are deserving of congratulation. While we appreciate the splendid efforts put forth by these hon. members, we feel that we cannot agree with their views with regard to the many debatable points which they have brought to the attention of the house.
It is now nearly four years since this government took office in 1930; this is the fifth session and we have had a fifth speech from the throne. Personally I have been keenly interested in reading the speeches delivered year after year by His Excellency since this government took office. I have noticed particularly that upon each occasion great care is taken to emphasize the efforts being made by the government to restore confidence and promote prosperity in our country. I do not think that I am in any way exaggerating when I say that great things were and still are expected from this government, and for that reason the eyes of the Canadian people, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, have been turned with expectancy and hope from year to year to the contents of the speech from the throne. That is particularly true this year, because, after all, hope deferred maketh the heart sick; and as far as the hopes that have been raised by previous speeches from the throne are concerned, I think the Canadian people, and indeed the members of the government itself, must admit that they are far from having been realized.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) has accused the Liberal party of trying to capitalize the present unrest and depression. I think it was unfortunate that he should be the one to make this charge, because I have a very distinct recollection of the right hon. gentleman himself, in 1930, going through the country from one end to the other making various speeches, and if ever anyone endeavoured to capitalize unrest it was the Prime Minister himself. It did seem to be the policy, the planned policy I should say, of the Conservative party during the 1930 federal election to endeavour to saddle upon the shoulders of the Liberal government all the responsibility for the conditions that existed at that time. It seemed to me that

every Conservative speaker and every Conservative candidate had been schooled to the fact that their duty was to attribute all our woes and ills and grievances to the government of that day. The depression that existed at that time was, in the expressed opinion of our hon. friends opposite, attributable to one source and one source only, and that was, as the Prime Minister himself described it, that band of mercenaries who had betra3'ed Canada for their own personal-gain. We all remember that famous statement, "Nine years before the great betrayal; it did not take Judas that long." That was the language used towards those who then occupied the treasury benches; that was the chivalry shown towards those who were bearing the responsibility of government at that time.
Now, the only comment I wish to make on that is this, that I sincerely hope the time will never come when I shall have to use language such as that with respect to our hon. friends opposite or anyone else. I think we ought to try to give those who do not agree with us with regard to our economic situation credit at any rate for honesty of purpose. We were all anxious, I am sure, to hear the speech from the throne this year to find out what new promises or what new hopes would be contained therein. Before going to previous speeches from the throne, I may say that during the 1930 campaign, while our hon. friends did endeavour to belittle and ridicule the government at that time, they also set themselves up as the ones who were able to lead Canada and the Canadians out of all their economic difficulties, and in order to convince the people that they were capable of doing so, many promises were made which have never been fulfilled but which I think have created such a burden for the government that it now totters beneath its self-imposed load.
It is a well known fact that this government took office with a tremendous burden of responsibility resting upon it. A large part of that burden, perhaps, was not of their own making, but I do think that the greater part of the burden was of their own making, owing to the many extravagant promises made; and while we know that these promises were almost, in fact quite, impossible of being carried out, nevertheless the government secured thousands upon thousands of votes by making them. I quite realize that the picture that was presented to the electorate during the 1930 campaign in regard to the situation which existed then, and which I think to a large extent no party was responsible for, was

The Address-Mr. Golding
that the Liberal party was to blame for all these conditions. It is certainly interesting to review the statements made by the government in their previous speeches from the throne. If we go back to the first session held under this administration, which opened in September 1930, we find in the speech from the throne the following words:
The necessity for dealing with exceptional economic conditions, with the resultant unemployment, has induced me to summon you at an earlier date than would otherwise be necessary. Measures will be submitted for your consideration, including amendments to the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff, which it is anticipated will do much to meet the unusual conditions which now prevail.
You will notice there that they refer to the Customs Act and the Customs Tariff, and at that session the government did introduce legislation which they believed would restore prosperity to the country. Indeed, they were simply carrying out their pre-election pledge to raise tariffs against all countries including Great Britain itself, and that of course they certainly did. Another important thing that was done then was the voting of some $20,000,000 for unemployment relief. In all fairness to the government, I am perfectly satisfied that they did believe that by putting into effect this high tariff policy, and by the action taken at that time, they would restore prosperity to our country-by using this $20,000,000 for the relief of the unemployed and by increasing employment through their tariff legislation, as well as by an effort to raise the prices of natural products. Indeed, I think they believed that by putting into effect their high tariff policy they were going to usher in for Canada a new and better day. After the close of that session, and with these new policies in effect, the people began to look with expectancy for the dawn of that better day, but to say that they were disappointed would be putting the situation very, mildly. In a few months another session rolled around, and on March 12, 1931, there appeared these words in the speech from the throne:
It will be your privilege to consider certain measures designed by my ministers to ameliorate existing conditions, to provide further means by which our people may go forward to achieve a prosperity heretofore unattained and to furnish them with all possible safeguards against a recurrence of the present subordination to world forces.
It goes on to say:
My government has explored the origins of our difficulties and is firmly of the belief that many of our problems do not arise put of world wide depression, but are antecedent to it; and that domestic factors have also largely determined the degree of economic distress from which this country is suffering.
If that statement was Drue then it is equally true now, and we on this side have endeavoured repeatedly to point out that domestic factors have largely determined the degree of economic distress from which this country has suffered during the past two or three years.
The statement was made prior to the election of 1930; it was made during the campaign and it has been made since, that the Liberal government in 1930 were not making any effort to meet the change in conditions which was taking place at that time. In direct contradiction to that I say that the then government fully recognized the fact that changing conditions abroad and existing conditions at home were affecting business in Canada, and to meet this situation they endeavoured to formulate a policy, one vastly different in spirit and details from that which was adopted by our bon. friends opposite at the short session of that same year. The Dunning budget was designed to cope with existing conditions and had certain definite objects in view which were made clear to the people by the members of the government at that time. By this an effort was made to divert trade, an action which was really forced upon the then government. Am effort was also made to lower the cost to the consumer, to lessen the cost of the implements of production to the basic producer and to lower the cost of raw materials to the manufacturer for export in order that he might be better able to compete in the markets of the world. Another vital point which had to be considered was the formulating of a policy which would at the same time assist in raising revenue. All these points were seriously considered by the them government, and notwithstanding all that has been said to the contrary, in my opinon the Liberal government did endeavour to formulate a policy which would cope with existing conditions at home and abroad. We all know that 'policy was never put into effect, and we on this side of the house and many people throughout the country feel that Canada was the loser by the change which took place.
It will be noticed that in the 1931 speech from the throne very little was said about world conditions; in fact our hon. friends opposite were at that time not talking about world conditions; it was the Liberal party that was responsible for everything. The speech of that year, after pointing out that the government had explored the origins of our difficulties and were convinced that many of our problems did not arise from world conditions, went on to say:

The Address-Mr. Golding

It was this belief which impelled my ministers at the emergency session of parliament held in September last to remove one of the root weaknesses in our industrial system by effecting such then possible changes in the tariff as would, in their opinion, provide substantial security against harmful world competition. Although in the interval world conditions have changed but little for the better, this tariff legislation has resulted in a marked improvement in the domestic situation.
That was part of the contents of the speech from the throne in 1931. In the third session which opened on February 4, 1932, we find the tone of the speech from the throne somewhat changed. It goes on to say:
World conditions are beyond the control of the Canadian people. But I rejoice that their resolute adherence to policies designed for the welfare of the nation has minimized the adverse influence of external economic forces. This period of trial has shown the Canadian situation to be fundamentally sound. . . . The provisions made at the last session of parliament for unemployment and farm relief are proving effective.
You are successfully meeting difficult domestic problems. Conditions are gradually improving.
In making his address a few days ago, the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber) stated that during the last few years about the best that could be said was to express a pious hope that conditions would improve. This is not an expression of any pious hope; It is a positive statement made in 1932 that conditions are gradually improving. Anyone who wants to be at all fair must admit that those words were not in keeping with the situation existing at that time. When we compare the prices which prevailed in 1930 with those which prevailed in 1932 and the number of unemployed as reported in 1930 with the number reported in 1932, we cannot help wondering how anyone could say that conditions were improving. There were only two reasons for making such a statement. The first, of course, was to try to raise the hopes of the people, and the second, and I think the principal reason, was to maintain confidence in the present government.
I quite agree that it really is important that every effort should be made to keep up the spirit and morale of a nation which has had to pass through such a period of depression as Canada has faced. I presume the government will expect us to excuse them on that ground for any unwarranted note of optimism that may have been expressed in their messages to the people given from time to time through the speech from the throne. I am not going to spend much time in adversely criticizing the speech from the throne for whatever note of optimism may be found therein. But I do think the members of this

house-indeed, the Canadian people-are keenly disappointed that the government has not offered any concrete suggestion of a policy which would have at least some effect in dispelling the gloom that has prevailed in this country for some time. The government has had splendid opportunities to do effective work; as a matter of fact it has had opportunities in a national and international way that perhaps few governments ever had. There have been conferences; there were two imperial economic conferences, a world economic conference, a conference with the president of the United States; there have been federal-provincial conferences. As a matter of fact this government has probably taken part in more conferences than any other Canadian government in a like period of time. Our Canadian people did expect some .beneficial results from these conferences, which certainly provided a splendid opportunity to get this much-advertised blasting policy into operation. But it is quite evident that the blasting machine was not functioning; so we have had large expenditures of money with very little result.

As one of the great exporting nations of the world I think we all realize that we need more and more markets. In this country we do not want any policy of extreme nationalization. I think we all realize that internationally we are all interdependent, and it has been pointed out by economists and statesmen that throughout the world more than a billion people are potential consumers of our surplus products, and that with the right kind of governmental policy they can be converted into actual consumers. All the great problems that confront this country at the. present time, including farm relief, agricultural surpluses, the utilization of manufacturing productivity, unemployment, the maintenance of our standard of living, our continued development and progress and international goodwill with resultant international peace, all seem to me to be bound up in this great problem of the expansion of our trade. Mr. Speaker, in continuing the debate on the speech from the throne I assure you, sir, that I have no intention of emulating or trying to excel some of the marathon speeches which thus far have been given forth in this chamber. The government has moved through its accredited representatives:
That an address be presented to His Excellency the Governor General, to offer the humble thanks of this house to His Excellency for the gracious speech which he has been pleased to make to both houses of parliament.
That is the formal motion which is now before the chair, and I congratulate the mover

The Address-Mr. Carmichael
(Mr. Gobeil) and the seconder (Mr. Barber) on their addresses in placing this motion before us.
From the official opposition has come an amendment to the main motion moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), as follows:
That the following be added to the motion: "We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's present advisers do not possess the confidence of the country."
There is no mistaking the intention of this amendment. It is a straight no-confidence motion and, of course, if carried would mean that the government should forthwith tender its resignation, and the country would be faced with a general election. From this corner of the chamber has come forth an amendment to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner), who leads the so-called Cooperative Commonwealth Federation forces-an amalgamation of farmer, labour, socialist forces, et al, we might say-called the Cocofeds out in our country. They have proposed that the amendment be amended by inserting after the word "advisers" the words "and official opposition". The amendment as amended would then read:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's present advisers and official opposition do not possess the confidence of this house or of the country.
Of course, this subamendment if carried would also mean the defeat of the government. It would even have a more far-reaching effect than that. It would mean that the country would have no confidence in either the Conservative or the Liberal forces to carry on government in this country, and the natural conclusion would be that the only force capable of carrying on the affairs of the state would be the representatives of the Cocofeds.
I have been listening to the debate thus far and had not proposed taking any part in it until this afternoon, and then I purposed doing so because I asked myself the question, what was going to be my own action when these various proposals were put before us for recording our vote. I represent a large rural constituency in that great agricultural province of Saskatchewan. I have a population of somewhere around 35,000. They are not all able to be here, and I think they expect me fairly well to represent what would be the majority wish of those citizens.
In order to put my position fairly before the house I shall have to go back a few years into political history and state that in 1921 I was first elected to this chamber under what was called the Progressive association
in our province. In my own constituency we had the Kindersley Progressive organization, which was affiliated with the Saskatchewan Progressive association. I was first elected under that organization known by that name.
In the general election of 1925 I was again elected by that same organization under the same name-Progressive.	In 1926 I again
had the honour of being elected by the people of that constituency as a Progressive. In 1930 our organization changed its name to the Saskatchewan Farmers Political Association, but it did not change its aims, its objects or its ideals. They were still the same as those of the old Progressive organization; that is, they were anti-party. They were opposed to contributions to campaign funds by moneyed interests largely for the purpose of holding a club over the party that might be elected to power. They maintained then, as they have always maintained, that each representative of the people should be elected and his campaign expenses paid by the contributions of the several electors caring to do so in the constituency. My four elections were run on that basis, and the expenses, I assure you, have been kept down to almost a minimum. In 1930 I came here representing practically the same organization, although under a different name, that I represented when I first was elected in 1921. This organization is not affiliated with the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, and therefore is not affiliated with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. The United Farmers of Saskatchewan have affiliated with this newer cooperative association. Therefore, as a representative of that constituency, I do not feel that I am bound by the actions of the United Farmers of my own province. Not being associated with them myself, and my organization not being affiliated with them, I naturally conclude that I am not bound to associate myself with all the views as propounded by the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation leaders.
While I have every respect for the farmer and labour representatives in this corner of the house and propose to cooperate with them in so far as I possibly can, I must say most emphatically that I do not share all of their views in regard to our present economic order, or that the best way out is in a complete change of that order. I do not share those views.
Not having any particular party leanings, not being affiliated with any particular party association, I have been led to inquire into just how I was going to express myself in the
The Address-Mr. Carmichael

votes which will soon be taken. I recall back in 1927, on February 14, I had the privilege of moving a resolution in this house as foh-lows:
That, in the opinion of this house, no government should have the right to ask for a dissolution of parliament prior to completing the five-year term as provided in the British North America Act except when authorized to do so by a majority vote of the house.
I still hold that view to-day as I did then, that it should be incumbent upon a government to fulfil its full tenure of office of five years when elected by the people and sent here to do so. I do not share the view that we should immediately, on the smallest pretext arising, seek to oust the government from office and call for a general election. It is true that there might be a change on the treasury benches, but it would be a change of personnel rather than a change of conditions in the country, it would seem to me. If we were to change the Conservative administration to a Liberal administration, granting that such a change might take place-I am not assured that it will-but even though it should, I would not conclude that that change of itself would remedy conditions as they exist in the country. I made it my business before coming down here to inquire of different citizens as to what their viewpoint was in regard to a prospective general election this year, and I did not hear one person, not one, either Liberal or Conservative or of any other political stripe, say that we should have a general election this year. So far as the persons whom I interviewed are concerned, it seemed to be their opinion that elections at best are disturbing and expensive, expensive to the country and expensive to the individuals who run their own elections; and of course there is unsettlement so far as business interests throughout the country are concerned. That being the opinion expressed by some of my electors, and having my own personal opinion, I feel that the government should run the full five years. Having no political axe to grind I feel that so far as my individual support is concerned, it is up to the government to carry on. If I were to support the subamendment as proposed, it would mean that I would be asking the government to quit immediately and the official opposition to get out of the way so that the representatives in this corner of the house could be given a chance to carry on. That is what I would be saying, but I do not propose so to say.

If I were to support the amendment to the main motion, in effect I would be saying that the government should get out of the way immediately and give the official opposition in its great zeal to save the country a chance to do so. I do not feel like saying even that. I still feel that the government is strong enough to carry on for the balance of 1934 and for that portion of 1935 which would be coming to them within their five year tenure of office.
While general conditions in the country may not be quite as bad as the leader of the opposition propounded to us in his four-hour and twenty-three minute speech on Monday, while they may not be quite as good as the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) outlined to us in his almost four hour effort in reply to the leader of the opposition, I do know that in my own constituency conditions are not good. Indeed they are very bad. In the rural municipality of Kindersley, a small local unit of administration, during the winter of 19331934 there are approximately one hundred families on relief and it is estimated that the total cost up to April 1 will be $10,000.

Approximately 1,500 in a nine-township unit. In the eleven or twelve-township unit of Newcombe, with a population of around 1,800, there are 188 families on relief. The secretary has advised me that the estimated cost for the 1933-34 winter up to April 1 next is $20,000. Other rural municipalities in my constituency are in practically a similar position. The town in which I reside is similarly placed with a number of families on relief. I want to assure the hon. member for Lanark (Mr. Thompson), who spoke this afternoon, that this is not because of the particular stripe of government in our province or governmental extravagances; I can assure the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner) that it is not because of the economic system under which we are labouring; the conditions which we are now facing are caused by what I think would be called in legal phraseology,- an act of God. We have had an absence of rain, we have had hot winds which scorched and blistered and blasted the crops. In many cases, what little did come through in spite of the drought was eaten up by the grasshoppers. As a result, in my own immediate vicinity the yields of wheat ran two, three and four bushels to the acre, and this only with raking and scraping and scratching. With the low price of wheat, hon. members will realize how much the farmer

The Address-Mr. Pickel
had to his credit after he paid his threshing expenses. There was practically no feed in the district, hay and oats being shipped in to be purchased by the farmers under the relief scheme. This is the condition in my territory and I know it is even worse in many other parts of Saskatchewan. I had the privilege of driving over a large part of the province during the past summer and through the southern part you could find no feed, no stacks and practically nothing growing green for miles and miles except Russian thistles.
I notice the speech from the throne makes this statement:
You will be invited to consider legislation for the establishment of a central bank.
I heartily favour the intention of the government to establish a central bank in Canada. Page 98 of the report of the royal commission which was appointed to inquire into banking and currency contains some suggestions as to certain main features of the constitution of a central bank for Canada. Section 4 states that the bank should have the sole right of note issue. I trust that in the legislation to be brought forward this feature will be adhered to. So far as my own opinion goes, I would prefer to see this central bank modelled after the Commonwealth Bank of Australia. Upon twro occasions I have spoken in this house with regard to the Commonwealth Bank of Australia and I recommend to the members of the government a careful study of the setup of that bank. It has had a successful operation for a period of over twenty years with each year showing increasing profits which have accrued to the state. It is distinctly a government owned and controlled bank and has the sole right of note issue in the commonwealth of Australia.
Last year we had in London what was termed an economic conference. It was internationally agreed at that conference that the metallic coverage of gold could be reduced from forty to twenty-five per cent without any country being considered as being off the so-called gold standard. I remember hearing a member of the government speaking over the radio, I believe it was the Prime Minister, make mention of that fact and state that if Canada took advantage of that provision we could issue an additional $100,000,000 of dominion notes and still be on the gold basis.
The speech from the throne also contains the following statement:
My government propose further to promote employment by expenditures on essential public works and undertakings throughout the dominion.
I should like to see these two statements linked up. I hope the government of the day will take it upon themselves to establish a central bank and give it the sole right of note issue and then put into circulation such a quantity of additional dominion notes as will take care of essential public undertakings. In so doing there would be no toll levied on the money put into circulation. We all remember that when the $35,000,000 was circulated-I believe it was less than two years ago-there was a toll of one per cent for two years exacted from the people of Canada by the private banking interests to pay them for putting that money into circulation. That was what it amounted to. There was the cost of the note issue, but the profit was one per cent on $35,000,000 for a two-year period, or $700,000, which went to the private banks for the expense of printing those notes. If that is done by our central bank, the money being circulated through that organization, which we hope will be established, there should be no such toll levied. The money could be put into circulation by paying the people who took part in public undertakings such as public buildings, bridges, highways, such as the completion of the trans-Canada highway, the deepening of the St. Lawrence, which has been talked of for some years, and the Peace River outlet, which has also been discussed in this chamber for some time. Such public undertakings could very well be carried out and paid for without the taxpayers having to raise any additional money by means of taxation. When such time comes, I assure the government and in particular the Minister of Public Works, so far as my own section of the province is concerned, I am going to be very bold in asking for some public works which will take care of the unfortunate situation as it exists in central western Saskatchewan and which will give employment to some of the people who are so very much in need of money. It will also tend to relieve the situation that now prevails in that part of the province.

speechtext:
In the first place, may I congratulate the mover (Mr. Gobeil) and the seconder (Mr. Barber) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
During the last session of this house the committee on agriculture was authorized to hold an investigation into the milk situation then existing between the producers and the distributors. Much evidence was adduced relating to the pernicious and oppressive methods adopted by the distributors in several of the large consuming centres of the do-
The Address-Mr. Picket

minion., and a report based on that evidence, of a highly condemnatory and scandalous nature, against the distributors was found and duly filed. I presume that as regards any real benefit that has resulted so far, from that investigation, the report has probably been systematically pigeon-holed, and forgotten in conformity with the usual procedure with respect to the findings of commissions. The evidence brought out by that investigation conclusively disclosed that the producer was being unfairly dealt with and exploited by the distributor, and further revealed the fact that the present system was simply creating a few millionaires in the city and driving thousands of farmers into a state of penury. This unholy and damnable condition of the farmer is being encouraged and maintained by our provincial and municipal authorities. They seem to treat the producer with contempt, while the distributor is fawningly looked upon as a representative of the big interests. It is perfectly useless to apply to these bodies for relief; it has been tried many times without avail: the distributors control the situation entirely.
On behalf of the dairy farmers I wish to express our thanks to the house for its courteous concession in granting a committee to hold that investigation. After persistent inquiry on the part of the committee, and much side stepping and mystical evasion on the part of the distributors, many startling facts were brought to light. And then the half has not been told. I am not going to take up the time of the house relating all the difficulties that the producers run up against, but I want to cite two facts that have come to my attention since the investigation was held.
In the first place, I am informed by reliable people that between the first of September and the first of May there is practically no surplus whatever in at least one large plant in Montreal; in fact, there is a shortage, a shortage so acute that the plant has to resort to the manufacture of synthetic milk to supply the deficiency. This milk is manufactured from milk powder. Furthermore, I am informed that in this same plant milk brought in by producers is often emptied into the receiving tanks for pasteurization and distribution. The farmer's can is then refilled with separated milk, buttermilk or this synthetic milk, a colouring substance being added to denote that the milk is unfit for human consumption, and it is returned, the farmer being compelled to pay transportation charges both ways, in addition to losing the entire value of his own milk.
[Mr. Picket}
I was under the impression that copies of the evidence and of the report were transmitted to each province with the request that they take action with respect to this unfair practice. How far that request has been implemented in the different provinces I am just at present unable to say, but in the province of Quebec the .government has appointed a milk commission, a body shorn of all power or authority, except as a matter of course the ability to draw down a good salary. They have been offering the farmer unnecessary advice, for instance dn regard to keeping a better herd sire, improving bis pasture, reducing the cost of production, making two blades of grass grow where one grew 'before and similar information of which the farmer was already well aware.
There were two ways in which they might have been of greater assistance to the producer. The first is this: in the month of May last the distributors offered SI .20 per 100 pounds for association milk. The producers did not see fit to accept that price. A conference was arranged, and after deliberation 'the distributors increased their offer to $1.35 for association milk. For the benefit of any hon. members who do not understand what association milk is, I may say it is the milk received from the farmer that is distributed and sold by the plant in quarts or gallons from house to house. The excess above this portion so distributed is called surplus milk, for which a much smaller price is paid, and it is the fluctuation in the quantity and the price of this surplus milk that plays such havoc with the farmer. After this offer of $1.35 had been accepted by the farmers, the usual result followed; the distributors simply increased the fictitious, so-called surplus quantity and the farmers received even less than they had been getting before the increase in price. I have in my room many statements by farmers, and I can get bushels of them throughout the country, but I am going to read only one or two in order to give the house an idea of what the fanners are receiving for milk.
I have in my hand a statement from a farmer who is shipping milk from West Sheffoid, Quebec. In the month up to June 15, he shipped 4,874 pounds of milk, for which he received $1.35 per hundred pounds for 3,800 pounds, and seventy cents per hundred pounds for 1,074 pounds. That netted that farmer just forty-five cents per hundred pounds or one and one-eighth cents a quart. In another instance a farmer shipped 8,420 pounds of milk. He received $1.35 per hundred pounds

The Address-Mr. Picket
for 2,500 pounds and for 5,920 pounds he received seventy cents per pound, netting him 45 cents per hundred pounds with transportation out, or one and one-eighth cents a quart. Those are fair samples of the way in which ithe farmers are being treated as regards their surplus milk.
Later on in the summer the distributors, not content with exploiting the farmer right up to the hilt, turned their tender attention toward extracting a few extra shekels from their consumers. The distributors get it both ways, coming and going. It is a great game; there is no other equal to it, with the same opportunity of displaying spurious generosity at someone else's expense. They first advertised amongst their consumers the fact that the farmer was hard up. That was no idle dream; the farmers are at the breaking point. The distributors spread propaganda amongst their consumers that on account of the dry season the pastures were short, grain was high and out of their great exuberance of friendship and brotherly love to the farmer, notwithstanding the fact that there is never anything but strife between them, much as they were reluctant to do so, they felt it their bounden duty to increase the price of milk one cent per quart or about forty cents per hundred pounds to help the poor farmer out. This was in the month of August. In this way they put the onus upon the farmer for this increased price, although the fact of the matter was that the farmer knew nothing about it and had asked for no special concessions from the distributors at the time, being in no way a party to this gesture supposedly in his behalf. When I first heard of this proposal I was amazed, but withal pleased as I thought perhaps the distributors had really undergone a change of heart and were going to try in a measure to work for the general advantage and atone for the injustices they had inflicted upon the farmer for many years. I could not quite get it out of my mind that there was a nigger in the fence, and this is how the scheme worked out: the price of milk was raised forty cents per hundred pounds; the distributor allotted fifteen cents of that to the farmer, and, according to his usual custom, kept twenty-five cents for himself. This is simply another example of the spurious generosity and double dealing of the distributor.
The milk commission of the province of Quebec could have rendered valuable service had they been so inclined. I noticed in the press during the latter part of the summer and in the fall several reports of the activities of the Hon. Mr. Godbout, Minister of Agriculture for Quebec. He made this statement on several occasions, but in one speech in particular, delivered in the county of Jacques Cartier just prior to the last election, speaking amongst other things of his paralyzed and incompetent milk commission, he said that at the next session of the legislature legislation would be introduced to deal with the milk situation, for instance, to give authority to set the price of milk so that the producer would receive an equal share of the customer's dollar. That is just what the farmer is looking for and what he is eventually going to have. It might just as well be done at once as later on. The farmer is entitled to a fifty-fifty division in the price at which his milk is sold. He will never be satisfied with $1.30, $1.40 or $1.50; he wants a percentage basis. When that is established no more will be heard of lost bottles which in the investigation were shown to range between $7,000 and $18,000 per plant per year, which the farmer unjustly pays for. No more will be heard of the abuse of price cutting indulged in by chain stores as an advertising expedient. No more will be heard of duplication of services and special services for which the farmer is called upon to pay.
Mr. Godbout further stated that the farmer must reduce his cost of production, and which, according to him, should not exceed 45 or 50 cents per hundred pounds. During the investigation we went into that point very thoroughly and established in the first place a cost of production of milk on the evidence of two gentlemen, Father Labelle and Professor Toupin, of Oka, who had made an intensive study of the question. On their evidence the cost of production of milk per hundred pounds was shown to be about $1.50; and that estimate included only the cost of labour, feed and care. But we had Professor Reynolds from the Ontario Agricultural College, Mr. Merriot, Mr. Fletcher, and Mr. Hughes, representing the different producers' associations in Ontario. They had made a particular study of the question, and they estimated the cost up to $2.50 per hundred pounds. In their figure they took into account overhead, interest on the investment of the farmer, taxes, aDd insurance. Yet Mr. Godbout proposes that the farmer produce milk at 45 to 50 cents! With all due respect to the hon. gentleman's opinion, I contend that is absolutely unreasonable and impossible.
I am not going to say any more about milk. I understand that in Ontario at the present time the government are proposing to stabilize the price of milk. If the province of Quebec will endow their milk commission with some power, and the commission will use that power for the benefit of the producer, I think it will
The Address-Mr. Picket

do some good. At any rate if the provinces do not act with expedition in this matter I would earnestly ask the federal government to assume or acquire the necessary jurisdiction to terminate for all time this perpetual cause of contention between the producer and the consumer.
There are other things that the farmer produces besides milk, and he is suffering just as much in connection with those different articles as he is in connection with milk, and is toeing imposed upon just as badly. How often we hear the favourite expression of candidates in rural constituencies, that agriculture is the basic industry of the country. It is heard oftener, of course, in rural sections than in urban centres. We hear it chiefly during election campaigns by the candidate and his followers, who meet the farmer like a long lost brother and gabble about the importance of agriculture, which in most cases, to the gabbler at least, is just so much hot air, a mere play of words, meaningless drivel. They tell the farmer that the country cannot get along without him. That is true, but the farmer has never been ingenious enough to capitalize upon that fact. The farmer is a peculiar toeing; he is by nature and temperament an individualist, and this innate peculiarity is largely responsible for his undoing. One of the chief characteristics of farmers as a class is disunion in their own ranks. This inbred disposition of the farmer is taken advantage of by the packer, the middleman and the commission man, in their finished and devastating technique for exploiting the farmer, whose industry is being constricted, compressed and strangled; graded, regraded, degraded and finally crucified by adverse government regulations and restrictive acts unfairly administered by the commission houses, contrary to the spirit of the framers of those acts and regulations.
Now sir, let us consider our home market for a moment and view its inner workings as controlled-improperly controlled-by the middlemen ; perhaps I am within my rights in saying illegally controlled. Yet that may not be quite right, because they are bolstered up by different restrictive acts that have been in existence for many years. This did not develop in a day; it has been going on for a long time; the farmer has been ignored for years. His interests have not been looked after by one party any more than the other. This is not a party question; it transcends parties, but it means the life or death of the biggest and best class of citizens in the country. I do not wish to imply that this special legislation was enacted with an ulterior motive
rMr. Pickel.]
against the farmer. I fully concede that these acts were probably decreed with the best intentions and presumably in the interests of the farmers, but the middleman has become a past master in their artful interpretation and administration. He has had a free course, a golden opportunity, and he has made the most of it. The temptation was alluring; there were no obstacles in his way, and he simply took advantage of the situation. It would be very interesting if we could get the full history of the framework of these different restrictive acts. I never heard that a farmer-producer was ever consulted in reference thereto; I have always associated their evolution with the combined efforts of technicians and heads of departments, at the request of shrewd middlemen. They have been enacted and put upon our statute books without in any way consulting the producers.
Our home market should be the best in the world, because we consume ninety-eight per cent of all our farm products at home, with the exception of wheat and cheese. But it is right here in our own home market that the farmer has been exploited and robbed; he is being robbed to-day right on his own doorstep by the distributors. To-day in the cities, sir, you will find the cold storage warehouses bulging with farm produce, though they are not bulging quite so much as they were because the produce has been unloaded to the public by degrees since the farmers stopped producing. These goods were bought up at very low prices, in many cases for less than the cost of production, and the prices were arbitrarily fixed by the commission men. Today they are being sold at huge profits in order to create millions for a few in the cities. Why should these huge profits redound to the middlemen alone? Some adjustment is in order, and it should be made without delay. If conditions are not remedied at once in the country our rural life is doomed.
Industry of all kinds is picking up, with the single exception of agriculture. The government does not seem to realize that the farmers constitute the biggest and best class in this country, and that if they are prosperous it will have a marked effect upon all other classes. The government does not realize that the farmers are the biggest purchasers of any class in this country. Every day the farmer has to buy goods. He has to purchase the same articles that are purchased by the ordinary citizen as well as a long list of expensive articles which are necessary in the pursuit of his calling. He has to buy wire, nails, roofing, cement, lumber and a long list of expensive agricultural implements and machinery such as cream separators, expensive

The Address-Mr. Pickel
stablefittings, and so on. And it must be remembered that these expensive articles must be replaced every so often; they detriorate very rapidly. The government forgets that the farmers are perhaps the largest class of employers in this country. If the farmers were receiving adequate remuneration for their labour and goods to-day they could absorb from half to three-quarters of the unemployment which is so rife in the country and about which all governments are very much concerned.
There are one or two things which I think our legislators have forgotten or overlooked for a long time. Perhaps it may be because of the natural modesty of the farmer or perhaps it may be due to the fact that he is patient and long suffering that he is not continually, in and out of season, harrassing the government of the day by adopting the same peremptory tone, tactful schemes and issuing the same dire ultimatums that have characterized one section of our agriculturists. We in the east have made the best of a bad job; we have kept on paying the demands of the west. The fact of the matter, Mr. Speaker, is that the government does not know just how to help the farmer. Our legislators are not familiar with the difficulties and grievances under which the farmer is labouring; consequently they do not know how to give him relief. It is high time they looked into the matter and gave the farmers the assistance necessary to enable them to market their goods. The mere assertion that agriculture is the basic industry of the country and therefore should be encouraged and assisted, which we always expect and hear in speeches from the throne, both provincial and federal, will not help the farmer one iota unless it is implemented by sane and useful action.
Here is the position of the farmer to-day, Mr. Speaker, in a nutshell. He does not ask for a dole or a bonus; neither does he ask that the price to the consumer be boosted. What he asks for is his just share of what his goods sell for. His great and insurmountable difficulty is the distribution of his own goods in his own market. I mentioned the goods that are in the cold storage warehouses at the present time, and which were purchased at very low prices which were arbitrarily fixed by the middlemen. In the city of Montreal five men meet every Tuesday; they say, "We will pay so much for butter this week", and that settles it. During the producing season of the farmers, in the late spring and summer, the prices are depressed and they remain depressed just as long as the producing season lasts; but after he has
finished producing and has no more to sell, up goes the price. It is simply manipulated by the middlemen. It does not seem reasonable that the farmers should be subjected to a thing of that kind. This recession of price in the spring and summer during the producing season, and later the augmentation of price in the autumn and winter by as much as one hundred or one hundred and fifty per cent, occur almost with clock-like regularity, and as I say, this price fluctuation is simply the result of price manipulation by the middlemen. I trust that the house will appreciate the perplexity with which the farmer is aimlessly and hopelessly drifting, and the necessity of our getting together and trying to do something for his relief. I sometimes think that legislators never stop to give the farmer a thought. If a commission had been appointed for the purpose of producing a plan for putting the farmer out of business quickly, I do not see how they could have improved upon the system that is in use today for accomplishing that object; for it is a fact that the farmer is being driven off the farm. Both these men whose statements I have read are no longer farmers; they have been driven out of farming.
Do our legislators ever pause and wonder why so few dairy farmers are paying income tax? Do they not think that the dairy farmer would be glad to be in a position to contribute to the revenue from this impost? Certainly, sir, the dairy farmers would be only too glad to be in a position to pay income tax. It is amazing that hon. members do not pause to inquire why it is that the dairy farmers, with individual investments ranging from five to fifty thousand dollars in plants, should not be in a position to pay income tax. While the farmer may not be paying income tax directly-I do not know of any farmer in my section who does, and I think it is a crime-nevertheless I firmly believe that the farmers are the biggest contributors to the income tax revenues of any class in this country, but they contribute the tax indirectly and the other fellows get the credit.
