speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in extending my sincere felicitations to the mover (Mr. Gobeil) and the seconder (Mr. Barber) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, may I say that in listening to their speeches I was impressed, as I am sure all hon. members were, by the diversity of the problems that we have to face in a country with such an immense area as Canada. The mover of the resolution spoke of the problems of the eastern townships, and was followed by the seconder, residing nearly three thousand miles away on the Pacific slope. Sometimes as representatives in this House of Commons we are criticized because of the long drawn out sessions. The first time I was in this house I asked myself why a session should be long, but it did not take me very long to realize that the main reason was that with 245 constituencies spread over such a great expanse of territory, with different conditions and varying problems in each, it was necessary for the members who had been honoured by the representation of a riding in this house to put before it the problems of his own region, because the prosperity or otherwise of any one section is bound to have its effect upon the country as a whole. That is the reason, sir, why I am perfectly at ease as I proceed to present some of the problems pertaining to our section of the country, more particularly those of northern Ontario.
The first problem with which I wish to deal is that of the railways. I listened very attentively to the splendid speeches of both the Prime Minister (iMr. Bennett) and the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), and I read them afterwards in Hansard. The Prime Minister in his speech made a statement which certainly will not be very favourably received in the northern sections of Ontario and Quebec when he criticized very severely what he called the lack of vision of Sir Wilfrid Laurier and of the people responsible for the construction of the transcontinental section of the national railway system of Canada as we have it to-day. He also made mention of the fact that we have in this country a population of 10,000,000 or thereabouts. Surety the Prime Minister should realize that the construction of that railway through the northern part of Ontario and Quebec is responsible for maintaining at least hundreds of thousands of people in that section of Canada. Let the right hon. gentleman try to visualize the condition of industrial centres like Toronto and Montreal without the population of northern Ontario and Quebec, who are their best customers. The

same thing applies as forcibly to the wheat growers of the three western provinces, and indeed to the whole of Canada. No doubt there was over-optimism, but no government could have foreseen what the railways would have to contend with in the future. No one could have foreseen the great development of the automobile industry and the competition of the motor truck and the autobus with our railways. I have in mind a statement made by Henry Ford a few years ago that it would soon be found that the countries which were the least railroaded would be the best off. But in this country, on account of our long distances and our climatic and geographical conditions, sheer necessity compels us to maintain our railroads and their identity; and they were a necessity for its development and expansion.
I listened with a great deal of interest to that part of the speech from the throne in which His Excellency says:
Since I have been associated with you as the representative of His Majesty in Canada, I have visited every province of the dominion. I have been greatly impressed by the loyalty, devotion and friendliness of the people, as well as the high courage with which men and women were meeting and overcoming abnormal difficulties in their daily lives.
It was with a great deal of pleasure that during last summer we had the honour of a visit in northern Ontario and Quebec from the representative of the king. It is true that for some reason which I know was absolutely unpremeditated, some of the larger centres of population were not visited. I have in mind particularly that wonderful new industrial centre of Kapuskasing, located on the Canadian National railway, and my hope is that if in the future we are honoured with visits from representatives of the crown they will find it possible to visit that fine centre of population. But the visit of His Excellency the Governor General would of course have been impossible without the opening up of that newer section of the country. What does it mean, the opening up of all this new territory in the Cochrane district, the Red Lake district, the Hearst district, the Amos and Rouyn districts and innumerable other sections which are traversed by the transcontinental railway running from Quebec to Winnipeg? All this was due to the building of the National Transcontinental railway from Quebec to Winnipeg. The spirit of optimism has always existed in the province of Ontario. When the provincial government contemplated building a railroad from North Bay northwestward to Cobalt, it is true there were people who doubted the wisdom of building

The Address-Mr. Bradette
such a road, but that capital expenditure has since been found to be fully warranted. Later on that ribbon of steel was pushed forward to Cochrane. Only two summers ago we had the wonderful spectacle of the opening up of the railroad from Cochrane to tidewater at Moosonee. Although that investment is not earning interest and amortizement, the province of Ontario is satisfied with the investment. It has proved to be one of the main sources of expansion, progress and prosperity in the whole province, and it has benefited the whole of Canada. Before the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) makes any more statements of that nature I hope he will find it possible to study the situation very thoroughly.
Take our own case in northern Ontario. We receive no direct benefit from the canalization of our waterways, but we feel that as long as it is beneficial to some sections of Canada, it has also an indirect beneficial effect upon our own section. The money invested in the canalization of our waterways is approximately $400,000,000. With an interest rate of four per cent per annum, this represents $16,000,000 per year. For the expense of upkeep there is expended annually about $3,000,000. The government does not receive one single cent in return, but there has not been a single word of criticism uttered in any section of Canada with regard to that expenditure. The government has seen fit to enter into a treaty with the United States to provide for the development of the St. Lawrence waterway. Without trying to prophesy, I have no doubt that that waterway will cost hundreds of millions of dollars when it is eventually carried out. I ask the Prime Minister to take this into consideration when considering these matters.
When discussing a matter of such importance as our railroads, every hon. member should consider the benefit derived therefrom by every section of the country. It is quite true that we have not received the attention we deserve in the exploitation of the National Transcontinental. It is true also that there are discriminatory rates from Winnipeg to Quebec which prevent any through traffic in freight or passengers on that section of the road. We made several appeals to the old railway board but we were unable to obtain justice. When the National Transcontinental section of the present government railway system was built, it was never intended for local traffic; it was intended primarily for through traffic, but because of the development of our natural resources, because of our riches in forests, waterpower, mines and agriculture, it is now found that this section is not only self-supporting but is one of the best-paying sections of the whole nationally owned railway system. I hope that my own section of the country as well as the northern section of the province of Quebec will again present their ease to the new railway board. We are confident that justice will be given to that particular section of the government railway system, and we believe that that faith will not be shattered.
I shall now deal with another matter which, although regional in its nature, has had its effect upon the rest of the country. I refer to the strike of the bushmen and settlers which took place last fall and is still continuing in certain sections of northern Ontario. It may seem strange to many hon. members that settlers working at lumbering operations have found it necessary to strike, but such is the case. No doubt hon. members have read the particulars of this strike which appeared in the newspapers. It lasted for weeks in the northern section of Ontario and spread past the Quebec border . I do not think it is for me to discuss the wisdom of the leadership of those men. As far as I am personally concerned, I have no love for some of the leaders, and the premier of the province of Quebec has shown that he has no patience with them. But there is no doubt in my mind that the bushmen and the settlers were suffering a great injustice in Ontario, and this applies equally to the province of Quebec. Although some of the leaders may have been radical, I think they deserve credit for the manner in which the strike was conducted and the results which were obtained. They found the men were not receiving justice and they formed an organization whereby the bushmen could air their views and have their grievances considered by the proper authorities. I know for a positive fact that there are members on the other side of the chamber who are still in their constituencies only because of the fact that some lumbermen are still on strike.
Before I proceed further with the matter, I should like to say a few words of praise for the attitude of most of the strike leaders and the officials of such centres as Kapuskas-ing, Cochrane, Ansonville, Hearst and others. A strange situation existed as far as Ansonville and Cochrane were concerned. The industries themselves were located quite a distance from these centres of population. What I have to say applies more particularly to Smooth Rock Falls and Iroquois Falls. These strikers were sheltered and fed by the towns of Ansonville and Cochrane. It is to the credit of the strike leaders that
The Address-Mr. Bradette

they always appealed for peacefulness among the strikers. The strikers behaved themselves and therefore received the support of all sections of the population. The national and international unions came to their rescue in order that the strike could be carried on, going as far as giving a part of their weekly wages. The first company which found it possible to settle with the men was the Spruce Falls company of Kapuskasing, and I think great credit is due to Mr. Noble, the general manager of the mill. But a different situation existed in the other industrial centres of Smooth Rock Falls and Iroquois Falls because of the fact that the company was in receivership. It was almost impossible for the strikers' committee to obtain access to the officials of the company, but I think it is to the credit of the officials of the receivership that they tried their utmost to meet the strikers.
In order that the house may be seized of the situation, I intend to cite some of the demands made by the strikers, most of which have been acceded to by the companies. There was practically no compfeint as to food. Complaints were made with regard to the sanitary conditions in some of the camps, but I believe these conditions have been remedied. Under the provincial legislation there is sufficient machinery to meet this situation. Another demand was for a monthly wage of $35 for twenty-six working days, plus board. The strikers were forced to compromise on this item. As everyone familiar with lumbering operations will understand, it is absolutely impossible to strike a flat rate of wages. Upon several occasions I spoke to the strikers and urged them to accept a schedule of wages whereby the inexperienced men would receive $26 per month, with the wages graduating to a maximum of S35. If my understanding is correct, an agreement satisfactory to everyone concerned has been arrived at.
The strikers asked for the recognition of camp committees composed of workers in the camps, and the right to hold meetings in the camps. Familiar as I am with all the conditions in the district, I know for a positive fact that an effort is being made to promote cooperation between the workmen and the company, and I was told only a few days ago by an official of one of the large mills in northern Ontario that the agreement was working to the entire satisfaction of everyone.
I will not discuss all the demands that have been made but, only a few of them. Demand No. 9, the men are asking that the wood be scaled twice a month and receipt given. This
[Mr. Bradette.J
demand is quite legitimate. I know of one man who had cut an average of ninety logs a day and when he received his scaling receipt at the end of the month his average was very considerably reduced. Obviously this is not satisfactory to the workman, and the situation must be remedied; scaling will have to be carried out in accordance with the requests made by the strikers.
The settlers, I may point out to the house, also took part in that strike, and some credit would seem to be due so far as the leaders of the bushmen's organization are concerned. Lumbering operations are extremely seasonal. Perhaps ninety per cent of the axemen and bushmen are farmers by calling. They spend only a few months, in fact the winter months, in lumbering, returning in the spring to their farming; at any rate, that is true of the majority of them. That fact alone will indicate how difficult it is to maintain a labour organization. However, the nucleus of a permanent organization has been established, which it is hoped will be maintained indefinitely.
The farmers also have their grievances, let us remember. In some instances there was violence, cars having been unloaded, loads upset, and so forth, but the settlers have cause for complaint, and they have formulated their complaints for submission to the company. In the first place, the settlers are asking, for four-foot pulpwood, $5 per cord, of which they suggest that $1.85 be paid in advance. It is not unreasonable that they should be given $5 per cord. Speaking to an Ontario minister last summer, I said that if the provincial government could find it possible to pay the settlers $5 per cord for the pulpwood they cut -that is, $5 at the siding during the coming winter the provincial government would have to spend practically nothing in direct relief. But what has happened? It is true that one corporation, before the snow came, and owing to the shortage of pulpwood, paid $5 a cord for a few weeks, and practically every settler along the Transcontinental, from Kapuskasing to Hearst, hauled pulpwood on the bare ground and found it remunerative; but the moment the snow came-and the snowfall there was premature, as it was in other sections

the company reduced their payment to $3.50. Now, everyone who knows anything about lumbering operations and the cutting of pulpwood will agree that the farmers cannot possibly make both ends meet if they are to receive only $3.50 for their pulpwood. At present some companies are paying $4, but I insist that unless a minimum of $5 is paid, it is absolutely impossible for the farmers to get along. It is no wonder the

The Address-Mr. Bradette
provincial government finds it necessary to keep up an expensive system of direct relief. The farmers are not being given an adequate remuneration for the pulpwood they are cutting under such difficult conditions.
It was with a good deal of interest that I heard the Prime Minister declare, the day before yesterday, that the pulp and paper industry is one of the greatest industries in Canada. We know how much capital is invested in that industry, and we know the amount of employment it gives to tens of thousands of Canadians. Lumbering operations, as I have already pointed out, are extremely seasonal, and in our section of the province-and this applies to the province of Quebec as well-these operations enable the farmers to balance their budget; it is an occupation from which they can add to their income. But we must remember that one of the best ways to bring prosperity to Canada is to give a fair remuneration to all workmen. The Prime Minister, when he returned from the world economic conference last summer, said that he was in favour of increased commodity prices. I would point out to him that this is not enough; along with increased prices there must be an increase in wages, and if wages axe not increased to keep up with prices there will be no prosperity in this country, at any rate not for some time to come. Just imagine the father of a family, getting $26 a month, and trying to keep that family, body and soul together, when he has to pay let us say $20 a month in rent. And in that northern climate fuel is an expensive item. I repeat, it will help matters considerably, and I hope that in every section of the country this will be realized, particularly in Toronto, if the government can find it possible to allow a minimum of $5 per cord to settlers. The settlers are also asking that their wood should be sealed at the time of loading and not at the mill.
There is no reason why the present situation should be tolerated any longer. A few years ago, when we were shipping carloads of pulp-wood to the United States as well as to Canadian mills, not a single stick of wood left the siding unless it was scaled. The farmers knew how much wood was in a car and they knew the price that would be paid; they simply awaited the return of the cheque. Under the present practice in regard to scaling the farmers do not know what they are going to receive, and they have every reason to protest and to maintain the strike until this grievance is removed. I know of settlers who have loaded a car containing sixteen cords of pulpwood, and anywhere R'ym two weeks
to a month afterwards they have received a scale of twelve or thirteen cords, losing sometimes as high as four cords to the car. Everyone will realize, from the facts as I have indicated them, just how unfair the system is. If it is true that occasionally settlers may have loaded bad wood on the cars, there is a method of remedying such a condition, but every stick of wood that is being shipped should be scaled at the siding. This is a matter of which both departments of labour, provincial and federal, should be fully seized.
I think we should be able to learn 6ome lessons and draw some useful conclusions from this strike. As representative of that district in this house I find myself in a peculiar position. Before leaving for the north country I had a conversation with the federal Minister of Labour, who promised to give all the help he could, and of whose sympathetic attitude to the settlers and strikers I had no doubt. But the moment I was among the strikers, the moment I endeavoured to act as intermediary between the company and the men, I found myself in a strange position. I found, for example, that there were two authorities each of which had a certain extent of jurisdiction. In several instances I found if not conflict at least overlapping between the two authorities. For example, there is an Ontario statute, the Disputes Act, which provides quite clearly that in the time of a strike the mayor of any towm or municipality may be sent by the provincial government as an official to try to solve the difficulty But, as I stated previously, we are in a singular position so far as Cochrane and Rouyn are concerned. Many strikers were residing within the limits of those towns and they were being sheltered and fed by those municipalities. We were not directly interested; I mean by that that the industry was not located within the borders of those municipalities. There is certainly overlapping of authority between the provincial and the federal Labour departments. I know the federal Minister of Labour must have found himself handicapped by some of the statutes of Ontario and that conflict of authority does not permit the settlement of strikes as quickly as should be the case. This is quite comprehensible. I cited my personal case and I believe the federal department was in the same position as I was; they did not dare to interfere in the matter until such time as the provincial authorities had found it impossible to work out a solution of the difficulty. I mention this so that the house may know that certain anomalies exist in our statutes. The provincial legislation is

Mr. Speaker, before directing a few remarks to the speech from the throne I would like to join with hon. members who have preceded me in congratulating the mover (Mr. Gobeil) and the seconder (Mr. Barber) of the address in reply. I very much regret to have to admit that I could not understand the speech of the former; it is my misfortune that I do not understand French. I did, however, appreciate the excellent speech made by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Barber). I thought it was a moderate' and reasonable speech, and I think it was enjoyed by every member of the house.
I would like to draw attention to the amendment to the amendment, moved by the hon. member for Acadia (Mr. Gardiner). According to that amendment the resolution as amended would read as follows:
We respectfully submit to Your Excellency that Your Excellency's present advisers and official opposition do not possess the confidence of this house or of the country.
I presume that at the close of this debate the house will be asked to pass upon this motion. First the members will be asked to vote as to whether they have confidence in the opposition, and I fear that the motion of the hon. member for Acadia will be supported. Then a vote will probably be taken upon the amendment proposed by my right hon. leader, and that will be defeated. I think it would be very interesting if after that a vote might be taken as to whether the third party has the confidence of the house or the country. Unfortunately the rules of the house I suppose will not permit that. We shall not be permitted to ask this house whether they have confidence in the third party. But we may at least ask the country. Perhaps it is not necessary, however, to ask the country, for already certain parts of it have pronounced their views on that subject. Nova Scotia answered a while ago in quite decided terms. A little while before that election I had a conversation with a very intelligent young Nova Scotian in my own district who had just received a letter from a friend in Nova Scotia. My



The Address-Mr. Butcher
neighbour of whom I am speaking is a very strong adherent of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and he told me that this letter he had received from a friend in Nova Scotia conveyed to him the glad news that Nova Scotia was going solidly for the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation at the provincial election, Well, it didn't; in fact Nova Scotia replied in almost needlessly harsh terms to their request for support and confidence. Then British Columbia answered, perhaps a little less emphatically but none the less decidedly; and finally Mackenzie. In Mackenzie constituency probably the ground was as favourable as any that could have been found in western Canada. The candidate was handpicked. Then I want to read a statement made by the hon. member for Acadia as follows:
As I am limited to forty minutes I have not at my disposal the time, for instance, to give an outline of the program of the United Farmers of Alberta; nor have I at my disposal the time to give an outline of the program of the Labour group and other groups affiliated with the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. I have not the time to discuss the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation platform, but we have given it to the world; it is open to anyone to know what that program is. The program of these different groups is available to all who desire to know exactly what we are aiming at. And that is something of which the people of Canada have no knowledge, as far as the Liberal party is concerned.

I want definitely to dispute that statement-both statements as a matter of fact. The people of Canada, those who are interested, have very definite knowledge of the platform of the Liberal party. On the other hand they have not equally definite knowledge of the platform of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation. Why? Because it seems to me that there is a different platform for different provinces. For instance we understand that in some parts of the country the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation stands for the socialization of all natural resources, including land. That was the program of the United Farmers of Alberta some few years ago. I understand that now it is no longer a plank in their platform. Freedom of speech is announced as one of the policies of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, yet we are told that in the province of British Columbia it was very definitely stated that there would be discipline of the members of the party as well as restriction of the right of the press to publish anything that was detrimental to the party. So that altogether I think it may truly be said that there are two misstatements-not wilful of course, but two misstatements in the passage I read. In the first place we have not, and the country has not, a definite statement as to the platform of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, and it certainly has a definite statement as to the policy of the Liberal party.
Now I want to refer to two short passages in the speech from the throne. The first reads as follows:
My government realize, however, that further increases in price levels are necessary to insure success to those engaged in agriculture.
This is undoubtedly true; I do not imagine that any person will question it. The prices of agricultural products certainly must be raised before there can be anything approaching prosperity for agriculture. There must be prosperity for agriculture before there can be prosperity for industry. But already there has been an increase in the price level of commodities, other than agricultural products, which is in excess of the increase in the price level of agricultural products. I have here a very excellent little publication published by the Searle Grain Company and called the Farmer's Index, in which it is stated that on December 15, 1933, wheat had a purchasing power of 42 per cent of that which it had in the year 1913-14, but that on January 15, 1934, this purchasing power had increased to 50 per cent of that of 1913-14. It is pointed out that while the price of wheat on January

The Address-Mr. Butcher
15, 1934, was 71 per cent of the 1913-14 price, the commodities purchased by the farmer were 25 per cent higher than they were in that year. That means that with any given sum to-day the farmer can purchase only fifty-six per cent of the commodities he could have purchased with that same amount in 1913-14.
I think here we find one reason for a great part of the unemployment that exists to-day. There is no doubt whatever that tens of thousands of farmers throughout the land need implements, farm tools, machinery of all sorts and lumber for building; they need clothing, boots and in fact all kinds of commodities that industry would be very glad indeed to supply. Already reference has been made to this fact, but may I say that in my own constituency during the recess I visited half a dozen or . more of those farmers who were regarded as prosperous. I talked over the situation with them, and I found that each of these men needed new machinery that he could not afford to purchase at the present time, as well as a hundred other things around the farm and home. Therefore if the wish expressed in the speech from the throne could be only realized, and the purchasing power of the farmers increased, at once a new impulse would be given to industry.
The question arises as to how it can be done, and here of course is where great differences of opinion will arise. The speech from the throne states:
You will be invited to consider legislation designed to facilitate the efficient and profitable marketing of live stock and agricultural products.
No doubt careful consideration will be given any proposal the government may bring forward, but a further question arises. Is there likely to be any substantial increase in the price of wheat so long as we have such a large carry-over? I am convinced in my own mind that our tremendous carry-over of wheat, which has been referred to by several speakers during this debate, is a continual threat to the wheat market, and that threat will not be removed until that surplus has been considerably reduced. I am going to make a suggestion to the government, and I hope that at least it will be considered. It may be thought impractical, but I believe that in time it may be found to be quite the opposite. Notwithstanding the fact that the wheat markets of Europe are so limited, and that some of them appear to be closed entirely, is it not remotely possible that some of those countries would be willing to barter manufactured goods for some of our wheat? I know that the suggestion will not meet with 74726-12J
approval on the part of many of our industrial concerns. I know that it may be said, for instance, that Germany and other countries have all the wheat they require, but I believe that practically every European country could take wheat on reciprocal terms. If we would say to some of these countries, "We will barter 25,000,000 bushels of wheat for manufactured products of an equal value," it is just possible that some of our surplus wheat could be disposed of. If our surplus could be reduced by that means I believe that would be the first step towards an increase in price.
There is another paragraph in the speech from the throne to which I should like to direct the greater part of my remarks. In the last paragraph I find these words:
You will be invited to consider, amongst others, measures relating to the Excise Act, the Companies Act, the Judges Act, and the Elections Act.
In particular I want to refer to those measures that will relate to the Companies Act. I think the time certainly has arrived when the companies acts of the dominion and the provinces as well need overhauling. One must admit, and we cheerfully do admit, that among the thousands of company promotions in the past the vast majority have been absolutely legitimate enterprises, reasonably financed and carefully organized. In most cases such companies have served a good and useful purpose. Doubtless many mergers also have been of a beneficial character. Of such mergers and such companies and their promoters I have no criticism to offer, and the remarks I am about to make certainly do not apply to them. But there have been other promotions and other promoters that certainly do not fall within the foregoing category, but are of an entirely different character. They have not served any useful purpose; on the contrary their operations have been distinctly detrimental to the interests of the public and absolutely disastrous to those individuals who have been induced to invert in the securities offered for sale.
I think most of us will admit that there are many grave weaknesses and many striking injustices in our economic system of to-day. We do not admit that this system should be scrapped; we do not believe it should be scrapped, but we do believe that these weaknesses and injustices should be remedied. I cannot imagine for a moment that even the stoutest apologist for our present economic system will deny the charges I have made, nor will he deny that many financial crimes have been perpetrated in the recent past by
The Address-Mr. Butcher

a very objectionable type of company promoter and a similar type of financier and financial organization, causing great loss and hardship and even the most acute suffering to thousands of investors, as well as resulting in a very great increase in the cost of living to the consumer. This is one of the outstanding weaknesses of our system; I refer to the ease with which some financiers have been able to exercise their predatory habits by taking control of certain essential industries in which their only interest is to bleed them white. Already this evening an hon. gentleman has made reference to the milk industry and the manner in which huge fortunes have been piled up by the people handling the milk while the producers have been reduced almost to beggary. No doubt there have been many times when the promoters of this kind of enterprise have been caught themselves in the maelstrom resulting from their operations. They have been caught in the net they spread for others, but that does not in the slightest degree lessen the enormity of their offences or render it any less necessary that the most stringent legislation should be enacted to prevent a repetition thereof.
When we come to investigate the reasons for many of these promotions we find that mainly there are three or four, the first being the desire to make huge profits out of stock manipulation through the organization, reorganization or merging of the companies concerned. Then, having promoted these companies, they demand of the management that they shall reduce the cost of production to the lowest possible point, chiefly by oppressing labour, with no intention whatever of passing the saving on to the consumer but rather that of seeking to exact the highest possible price, make the largest possible profit, control the market and eliminate as far as possible all competition, by any means whatsoever, legitimate or illegitimate. There is no doubt whatever that if not actual fraud something

No doubt these men have been induced to form these various companies because of a general and somewhat natural desire on the part of the public to amass wealth quickly, .and they have taken advantage of this desire in order greatly to enrich themselves. With that lack of mercy which is peculiar to the tiger and the wolf, with the cunning of the fox, with fair promises on their lips but foul designs in their minds, they have set out to defraud and cheat the investing public. I know these are strong terms but they are undoubtedly true, and I am quite sure that many hon. members can think at this moment of instances of this kind of thing.
During the past few years there has been, as [DOT] has already been mentioned in this house, a great increase in the number of huge incomes in the United States-the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) made a reference to this yesterday. All this happened in one year, according to the United Staites income 'tax returns as published by the Internal Revenue Department. In 1928 there were 26 people with an income of $5,000,000 and over, as compared with eleven in 1927. I know that hon. gentlemen will say: "Why mention these things here? They do not apply to Canada; there is nothing like that in this country." There is no reason to believe that that kind of thing has gone on to the same extent in Canada, but it would be interesting to know to what extent less it has been happening here. The evidence already given before the Senate committee in the United States has been a terrible indictment of high finance in that country, and one wishes that a similarly exhaustive inquiry might be made into the history of some of our own enterprises, Canada Paper and Power, for instance. The financial brigands of whom I am complaining have in many instances chosen for their operations the necessaries of life and the minor luxuries for which there is a great demand. They have selected bread, fruit, fish, milk, coal, cotton, wool, pulp and paper, cement, asbestos and radio. Everywhere they dip unholy hands into the life stream of the people. Nothing is sacrosanct to them if by any means, be they ever so foul, they may enrich themselves at the expense of the public. This house has a duty with respect to these men, and I am hopeful that the government when it brings down amendments to the Companies Act will provide restrictive measures against this kind of thing. If that duty is neglected a day of reckoning will surely come, and it may take a form distasteful to most hon. members. The patience of many of our citizens is well-nigh exhausted; they are 'becoming better informed. If we fail to rise to the occasion, we cannot justly complain if we are replaced by other men who will deal with the matter.
During the dying days of last session I placed several questions on the order paper and received answers, and I am going to read these questions and answers because I want to make an explanation of my reason for placing the questions on the order paper. The first question was:
1.	Was a petition for an inquiry under The Combines Investigation Act alleging that an illegal combine consisting of: Canadian General Electric Company Limited, Canadian Marconi Company (limited liability), Canadian West-inghouse Company Limited', Northern Electric Company Limited, Western Electric Company Limited, Standard Radio Manufacturing Corporation (now the Rogers-Majestic Corporation), Canadian Radio Patents Limited, is operating and has operated since January 19, 1927, filed with the registrar under the Combines Investigation Act, during the year 1930?
The reply to that question was "Yes." The next question was:
2.	Did the registrar make an investigation and report to the minister?
The answer was "Yes." The third question was:
3.	Was the report of the registrar of such a character as to induce the minister to transmit the complaint, the petition, copy of the evidence taken at the investigations and other necessary documents to the Attorney-General_ of Ontario for appropriate action under section 31 (a) and (b) of the Combines Investigation Act?
The answer to that was "Yes." The next question was:
4.	In view of the fact that the Attorney-General of Ontario did not institute proceedings against the alleged illegal combine, has the minister considered the advisability of applying any of the other remedies enumerated in section 31 of the Combines Investigation Act. and what decision has he arrived at in connection therewith?
The answer to that was "Yes, but no further action is contemplated."
I shall now refer to a few of the allegations made in the petition for an investigation filed with the registrar of the Combines Investigation Act in connection with the alleged combine alluded to in the questions I have just read. I shall remark first, however, that of all the pernicious and, in my opinion, financially immoral ventures to which I have referred, this least touches the actual necessities of life. Nevertheless it is an example, though not the best that might be afforded, of that rapacious greed which characterizes the actions of many of the men whose names are almost invariably found upon the list of those most interested in this sort of enterprise. May I be permitted, Mr. Speaker, to inform you and the house of some of the outstanding features of this particular alleged illegal combine?
In June, 1930, a declaration alleging the existence of an illegal combine was regularly filed with the registrar under the Combines Investigation Act. The dedarant, one Charles Ridgway Gilpin of the city of Niagara Falls, in the county of Welland and province of Ontario, declared that a combine was then operating and had operated throughout the Dominion of Canada since January 19, 1927, for the manufacture and sale of radio sets and radio vacuum tubes. It was said that the combine consisted of the companies which I have already named. The petition alleged further that the Canadian Radio Patents Limited was incorporated by and on behalf of the other companies which I have named, with the addition of the Western Electric Company Limited. It was alleged that this

The speech from the throne also mentions that the resolutions of the World Economic Conference will be submitted to the house. It is therefore difficult to discuss at length the subject, because we are informed that amendments to the Bank Act and monetary system will be later on submitted. We must neces-arily wait to find out what a central bank means and know what changes will be made in the quotation of our present currency, as compared with what it is now on the basis of gold which we still retain under our present financial legislation. We must necessarily await the bringing down of such legislation so as to be correctly informed of what the house will have to consider.
Further on, the speech from the throne refers to a measure so as to curtail wheat seeding. I wish to frankly admit, sir, that a number of farmers from the southern and eastern sections of Ontario rejoice in seeing that the Dominion had at last understood the farmer's problem by giving a bonus of 5 cents per bushel, in 1932, on all Western wheat, because it was only fair that the growing of certain products, especially wheat, should afford a livelihood to its farmers, and, therefore, the government came to the rescue of those who carried on this production. When however, to-day, so as to solve the problem of those who carry on such wheat growing, they are requested to reduce, in the future, the acreage sown, it affords very little hope of improvement to the farmers of Canada, Ontario and Quebec. However, again do I state that one must necessarily wait. The government also leads us to hope that a measure in connection with agricultural short term and intermediate credits will be brought down so as to help the farmer. The latter is certainly in need of this credit and this, in various ways; however, if we are to judge from the statement made by the right hon. Prime Minister, in answer to the leader of the opposition's (Mr. Mackenzie King) question, the other day, it will be very difficult for the farming classes to obtain such credits, either in cooperation with the government or in cooperation with our financial institutions. He stated:	who,
among you, after all, would loan money to someone who is wholly insolvent or is on the eve of becoming so?
I am sorry to state, sir, that the farmers whom I have the honour of representing-for the county of Prescott, with the exception of a small industrial town, is essentially farming-are absolutely in the situation described by the Prime Minister. We took much pride in the past in the fact that the farming class was the foundation upon which rested the

entire economic structure of our country and that the labouring classes were certainly those who purchase the largest quantities both of the manufactured and agricultural products. I really wonder whether one can find in the speech from the throne, such as delivered to us, any hope of relief. It is true that one finds a little further on, that works are to be undertaken toward the relief of the unemployed, in the course of the year. I shall refer to this subject later, as well as to another in connection with agriculture to which the speech from the throne makes reference.
The speech from the throne further states that we shall be given an opportunity to study the Excise Act, the Judges Act, the Companies Act and the Elections Act. I shall not dwell further on that part of the speech. However, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) on the able speech he delivered as regards the necessity of amending the Companies Act, so that the various companies, holding either dominion or provincial charters, be so organized that they will only issue stable values to the public, and that the act be so drawn up to protect the interests of those who invest money in such enterprises, thus preventing speculation and informing the public of the real value of their shares or bonds previous to being put on the market.
Mr. Speaker, I do not think I can err much in repeating what was so well stated by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Pickel) that, of all classes, the agricultural one is certainly the class which is undergoing the greatest hardships and meeting the most difficulties. The speech from the throne sufficiently and very clearly states on this subject:
The prices of agricultural products which have fallen in recent years to the lowest level in history, have shown substantial improvement in the last few months. My government realize, however, that further increases in price levels are necessary to ensure success to those engaged in agriculture.
In fact, if we compare farming products with those manufactured, and if we take as a basis of comparison the year 1926 when the values of products were practically normal, when the farmer could fairly well balance his budget, and when our industries, trade and all other activities in the country were prosperous, I think we can well refer to the figure 100 as an indication of the value of these products. Therefore, basing our calculations on the year 1926, we find that the farmer would have required the amount of products which I shall mention shortly to purchase one dollar of manufactured goods. Taking

The Address-Mr. Bertrand
the figure 100 as our basis of comparison for 1926, the farmer could purchase $1.00 of manufactured goods in 1926, with $1.00 of farm products. In 1927, he could purchase $1.00 of manufactured goods with 95 cents of farm products. In 1928, $1.00 worth with 94 cents. In 1929, $1.00 of manufactured goods with 92 cents. In 1930, $1.00 of manufactured goods with $1.06. In 1931, $1.00 of manufactured goods with $1.33. In
1932,	$1.00 with $1.44 of farm products. In
1933,	$1.00 of manufactured goods with $1.38 of farm products.
Therefore, in 1933, last year, the farmer was forced to sell $1.38 of farm products so as to purchase $1.00 of manufactured articles, namely a drop of 38 per cent in the value of his products. The farmer must necessarily purchase a great number of articles which he does not produce on his farm. I must add that the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi stole a march on me with reference to the remarks that I intended to make so as to prove the difficult situation of the farmer. I, however, wish to congratulate the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi on his courage. In spite of what is disclosed in the speech from the throne, in spite of his leader's policy, and notwithstanding that he is a government supporter, he admits that there is nothing of any consquence in the speech from the throne, not an iota, that this question should be considered outside of party politics, because the farmer is at the door of bankruptcy and he must absolutely be assisted.

speechtext:
Truly,
sir, we cannot have more convincing proofs in this matter than those given by the hon. member for Compton (Mr. Gobeil). Referring to the price of butter, when he moved the address in reply to the speech from the throne, he stated that, in 1929, butter was worth 39 cents in Canada, while in the United States it was worth 45 cents; and he added that, in 1933, butter was worth 20 cents in Canada, while American butter sold at 21
cents on the New York market. He asserted that we had made a great gain since the difference was much less between the price of butter on the Canadian and the United States markets. However, the hon. member for Compton forgot to state that the fixed charges of the farming class are the same as those of 1930, at the time of the Dominion election when all Conservatives taking their cue from their leader, felt sorry for the Canadian farmer, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, they stated that something had to be done to enhance the price levels on agriculture. Today, although the farmer's lot is the same as in 1930, so far as his debts and liabilities are concerned the hon. member for Compton will allow me to prove, according to his own figures, that the price of butter has decreased 18-70 cents per pound. I do not think that such was the expectation of the farmers, when they listened to our friends proclaiming their policy in 1930.
It is, therefore, not amazing that, to-day, the government states in the speech from the throne:
You will be invited to consider legislation designed to facilitate the efficient and profitable marketing of live stock and agricultural products.
We welcome such a statement; however, as we are all aware that agricultural products in the world's markets fall under the inevitable law of supply and demand, the statement seems to us as having been inserted in the speech from the throne in view of a probable election in the course of this year. It is a clever way of renewing the pledges of 1930, and, in my opinion, we are greatly reminded of the promises of 1930; for instance those made by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), then leader of the opposition.
At Woodstock, N.B., on July 2, 1930, he stated:
I regret to see the deserted farm lands of New Brunswick. Quebec and other provinces. Well, I am going to say right here that I shall regard it as my great responsibility if elected on July 28 to see that the collective weight and power of the Dominion of Canada is placed behind agriculture. I would be lacking in qualifications entitling me to head a government if I failed to do so.
We are told, at times, that this pledge was fulfilled since the national market was reserved for the Canadian farmer and that it helped to safeguard the interests of the farming classes. I openly state, sir, that this explanation will not satisfy the farming community of this country, even if some of these pledges have had the honour of being

Ottawa. Our workmen protested against this policy because it was one of the few opportunities given to them to earn enough to support their family. We most earnestly protested and immediately requested that people from the district be employed when such works were undertaken rather than having recourse to workmen brought from distant points. The more so because our people are in receipt of money provided by the unemployment fund, while work is being done at their door.
I had a few other remarks to make, but I notice that the time allotted to me is almost at an end. I shall state in closing my remarks that the people of this country are anxious for a change of government in order to give the workmen a better opportunity of earning a livelihood and the farmer a chance to return to his normal state. We contend that they suffer the most in the present crisis and I can assure you that they desire the reestablishment of a better economic equilibrium among the various classes of society, the free intercourse of our international trade and an opportunity for each individual to occupy his normal place in the midst of our population.
On motion of Mr. Maloney the debate was adjourned.
